accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: The site number is a sequence of characters that identifies a single site, a unit of analysis that corresponds to various kinds of structural and spatial entities. Most site numbers used in this database correspond to designations used to label sites in the Millon et al. (1973) mapsheets.
accdbMetadata_PriorChangesToVar: Small numbers of sites have been subjected to post-fieldwork merging, and/or redesignation. This is much more common with subsite, rather than site designations, however.
accdbMetadata_Comments: Most sites correspond to single tracts of land ('collection tracts') that were used as the minimal unit of description, collection and analysis by the TMP. Some sites subsume one or more 'subsites', and in such cases, the subsites usually constitute the collection tracts that were defined and used by fieldworkers.Most sites were defined on the basis of visible architectural remains; a minority are based on spatial units that relate to recent or modern land-use practices. Site numbers are mostly integers, but some sites have the prefix "L". This indicates that the site was judged to lack significant evidence for occupation during the Teotihuacan Period, although there was evidence of earlier and/or later occupation; these determinations were sometimes later revised. Published references to TMP sites and subsites may use colons and subscripts that are not part of this database. A site designation such as 1B':N1E1 is composed of three parts: site 1; subsite B1; and square N1E1.
DF8Metadata_Text: Site Number. A sequence of three characters, including blanks, corresponding to the identification in Millon, Drewitt, and Cowgill (1973). Usually, the only non-blank characters are numbers (right-justified), but sometimes the first character is "L."
DF9Metadata_VarText: Site Number Within Sector. Within each 500 by 500 meter sector of the TMP map grid, sites were numbered, starting from 1 (often for a site judged unusually interesting or well known) to some maximum number. Rarely, for various reasons, a number was skipped. Because sites were defined without regard for the edges of the arbitrary map grid sectors, some sites extend spatially into two or even three sectors. These were generally numbered as part of the sequence within the sector in which they mainly occur, but in a few cases a site that is mostly within one sector is numbered as part of the sequence for a neighboring sector. For example, site 37:N5W1 is actually within sector N5E1. As explained in Chapter One, site numbers were generally assigned in the order in which sites were surveyed, but, for various reasons, survey sometimes jumped from one part of a sector to some distant part, so sites with numerically close IDs are not necessarily spatially close to one another, although they often are. Tracts that were initially judged to have significant amounts of pre- and/or post-Teotihuacan period materials were prefixed with the letter L, in a second numerical series – L1, L2, etc. In some cases, these initial interpretations were changed, and a few sites with the "L" designation were judged to have had significant Teotihuacan Period occupation, while a few other sites lacking the "L" were judged to have not been occupied or utilized during the Teotihuacan period. Users of this file should never rely on presence or absence of an "L" in this field as a secure indicator of Teotihuacan Period occupation. It is better to rely on other data fields and the "interpretations" sheets of Millon et al. (1973). Even so, there are some ambiguous cases, hopefully to be resolved eventually by excavations or other additional data.

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: Alphanumeric code for identifying parts of a single site that were recorded individually, as well as related collections and code sheets.
accdbMetadata_PriorChangesToVar: A fair number of subsites have been subjected to post-fieldwork merging, and/or redesignation. This may sometimes be a cause of discrepency between the current database and its various predecessors.
accdbMetadata_Comments: NEED TO REMOVE SPACES!!; NEED TO MOVE SECONDARY SITES FROM SUBSITE COLUMN (alongside "+" and "&") TO SITE COLUMN;; Subsite designations were used to identify survey tracts, collections and records thought to relate to a single 'site', but which (for one of several possible reasons [Millon 1973:22]) were treated as individual collection tracts. The subsite field is blank for most cases, since many collections from sites and subsites shown as single structures in Millon et al. (1973) were merged. The field is still relevant for subsites that were interpreted as distinct structures and left unmerged.  Published references to TMP sites and subsites may use colons and subscripts that are not part of this database. A site designation such as 1B':N1E1 is composed of three parts: site 1; subsite B1; and square N1E1.
DF8Metadata_Text: Subsite. Var. 2 is blank for most cases in DF8. It was originally used mainly for identifying separate code sheets for collections from multiple tracts of a single site and/or multiple collections from a given site. In DF8, most collections from sites and subsites shown as single structures in Millon, Drewitt, and Cowgill (1973) have been merged. However, subsite ID is still relevant for subsites interpreted as distinct structures and not merged in DF8. This variable is also sometimes used to indicate or at least suggest what was done when two or more sites that were given separate site IDs on the published map are merged (for reasons discussed on p. 2) in DF8. Occasionally, an otherwise mysterious digit in the rightmost space of var.2 is a survival from an indicator of a repeat collection on the original code sheets.
DF9Metadata_VarText: Subsite ID. This data field is blank for most DF9 cases. Sometimes, however, different tracts that share the same site number (data field 1) have been interpreted as representing different structures and appear as separate cases in DF9, distinguished only by having distinct subsite IDs. Sometimes the subsite ID has a fairly obvious interpretation, such as NW for the northwest part of the site, but often the subsite ID will be a seemingly arbitrary string of up to four characters. Many of these are the result of trying to suggest some complex merging of units originally described as separate during the field survey, within the limits of a 4-character fixed field. In a few cases an otherwise mysterious digit in the rightmost space of this data field is a survivor, not edited out, of an indicator on the original code sheet of a second collection from the same tract.

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: A four character designation for a 500m square containing the site or subsite. These squares were based on a grid system established near the beginning of the TMP survey, with its origin near the southwest corner of the Ciudadela. The first two characters indicate the square's position north or south of the origin; the second two characters indicate its position east or west of the origin (eg. N5W4, S2E6).
accdbMetadata_Comments: Published references to TMP sites and subsites may use colons and subscripts that are not part of this database. A site designation such as 1B':N1E1 is composed of three parts: site 1; subsite B1; and square N1E1.
DF8Metadata_Text: Map square designation. N2W8, S3E7, etc., as on the published map.
DF9Metadata_VarText: Map Sector ID. These are the 500 by 500 meter (25 ha) sectors of the TMP map – N2W8, S3E7, etc.

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: This is the distance from the center of the site north or south of the center of the Teotihuacan map grid (the SW corner of N1E1), in multiples of 10 meters. Negative numbers are south, positive are north: 467 means ca. 4670m north, -211 means ca. 2100m south.
accdbMetadata_Comments: NEEDS TO BE MULTIPLIED BY 10!!!!
DF8Metadata_Text:
North-south location of site. Distance of the center of the site north or south from the center of the Teotihuacan map grid (SW corner of N1E1), in multiples of 10 meters. Negative numbers are south, positive are north. Thus, 467 means ca. 4670 m north, and -211 means ca. 2110 m south.Very useful for spatial analysis. Using the Pythagorean theorem, the geometric distance between any two sites is readily computed:  
\[ D = \sqrt{(10 \times \text{var.4})^2 + (10 \times \text{var.5})^2} \]. They are also quite helpful for locating sites since, within a 500-meter square, there is often no obvious relation between site number and spatial location. -999 = missing data
DF9Metadata_VarText: North-South Location. This gives distance of the unit's midpoint from the center of the TMP map grid, which is at the southwest corner of sector N1E1, in multiples of 10 meters. For rectangular collection tracts, the midpoint is the center, which is also the centroid. Centroids of highly irregular tracts were probably estimated, but there was rarely any difficulty in doing this to the nearest ten meters. Negative numbers are south, positive numbers are north. Thus, 467 means ca. 4670 m north, and –211 means ca. 2110 m south.
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: North-South and East-West Location of Site: These two data fields are essentially the Cartesian coordinates of site midpoints, expressed in multiples of 10 m (change to actual meters?). Using the Pythagorean theorem, the straight-line distance between the midpoints of any two sites, i and j, Dij, is the square root of [(var.4i - var.4j)2 + (var.5i – var.5j)2]. This is very useful for many spatial analyses. Also, because site ID numbers (data field 1) often have no simple relation to their position with a sector, data fields 4 and 5 can be useful in locating specific sites, although this can be done more easily by a query that highlights the specific site on the map display. (Ian, is this right? Is there a better way to say it?)

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: This is the distance from the center of the site east or west of the center of the Teotihuacan map grid (the SW corner of N1E1), in multiples of 10 meters. Negative numbers are west, positive are east: 250 means ca. 2500m east, -420 means ca. 4200m west.

DF9Metadata_VarText: East-West Location. Defined the same way as north-south location. West is negative, east is positive.

DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Field Workers. DF8 was set up in such a way that it is not made explicit who had what role [also true of DF9?], and this is also not always entirely clear on the Site Survey Records (SSRs). Persons who were typically or always crew chiefs include Matthew Wallrath (1,050 cases), Bruce Drewitt (752 cases), Michael Spence (596 cases), James Bennyhoff (565 cases), René Millon (254 cases), Joseph Marino (251 cases), Charles Kolb (226 cases), and George Cowgill (150 cases). Beginning in 1965, Pedro Baños (3,326 cases, including those where he was a crew member) was usually a crew chief, but not before. Persons who never or almost never were crew chiefs include Arnulfo de Lucio (2,654 cases), Silvestre Sánchez (1,440 cases), José de Lucio (1,348 cases), Daniel Hungerford (212 cases), Clara Millon (102 cases), Dan Bruhns (75 cases), Silvia Duran (57 cases), Mario de Lucio (44 cases), James Dow (35 cases), Jane Quisenberry (31 cases), Karen Bruhns (12 cases), Paul Shankman (6 cases), and Michael West (3 cases). Cowgill is uncertain about the number of sites for which Steve Sharnoff (472 cases), Donald Sutherland (334 cases), Warren Barbour (256 cases), Darlena Blucher (215 cases), Jeffrey Wilkerson (139 cases), and Charles Fletcher (133 cases) served as crew chief rather than student assistant. A good indicator that one of them was likely crew chief is the absence on the SSR of any of those listed above as often a crew chief. Sometimes the order in which initials are listed on the SSR can be a clue, as is handwriting, although the SSR was often filled out by a student assistant rather than the crew chief.
RC_VarDesignProblem_Comments: Change to Presence/Absence for each person;; This would mean converting these 5 variables into 32 boolean variables (one for each field worker) -- or 29 boolean variables if excluding the 3 of 32 personnel that are not present in any row

accdbMetadata_Comments: Collections made in December are coded for the following year.
DF8Metadata_Text: Last two digits of year collection made. December of each year gets assigned to the next year. Thus, a collection made in December 1964 is coded "65."
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Year and Quarter of Collection. Most collections were made between 1962 and 1967, with 311 in 1962, 286 in 1963, 836 in 1964, 1,406 in 1965, 1,216 in 1966, 888 in 1967, 66 in 1968, 1 in 1969, and 4 in 1970). Data field 11 gives the last two digits of the year, with December of each year assigned to the next year. Thus, a collection made in December 1964 is coded "65." Data field 12 gives the quarter of the year in which the collection was made. Those coded "1" were made in December through February (915), "2" means March through May (803), "3" means June through August (1,972), and "4" means September through November (1,319). Joint use of these two data fields makes it easy to pin down the date of the collection by 3-month period. In cases where two collections made at different times were merged, we have to look up how this was handled. SSRs give the exact day(s) of the survey and collection.

Those coded "1" were made in December through February (915), "2" means March through May (803), "3" means June through August (1,972), and "4" means September through November (1,319). Joint use of these two data fields makes it easy to pin down the date of the collection by 3-month period. In cases where two collections made at different times were merged, we have to look up how this was handled. SSRs give the exact day(s) of the survey and collection.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Last major Teotihuacan building phase.  DO NOT RELY ON THIS DATA FIELD! (Possibly omit it from the version for distribution.)  It was supposed to have been based on a sensitive reading of the SSRs. However, few SSRs discussed this question explicitly, and in practice coders relied almost entirely on a very mechanical interpretation of sherd counts, which could have been done as well or better by looking at data fields 205-217, and still better by looking at the "interpretations" maps of Millon et al. (1973). In addition, a programming error in creating DF8 (the predecessor to DF9) changed all the "missing data" values for data field 13 to zeros, thereby losing the few (if any) sites judged to have no major Teotihuacan building phase later than Patlachique. Note that the latest building phase is not necessarily the latest phase of significant occupation. Millon (1973:___) thinks that many substantial structures may have continued to be occupied somewhat later than the last phase well represented by surface debris because collapse of walls and roofs would have buried the material actually in use during the latest occupation of the site, but left re-used construction fill exposed. Cowgill is doubtful that material from the last significant Teotihuacan-period or later occupation phase of substantial structures is often absent on the surface, if any material at all is visible. Both Millon and Cowgill think that materials from the latest occupations of sites without substantial structures are likely to appear on the surface. In spite of all these reservations, data field 13 may be of some use in identifying sites that perhaps were not occupied in later parts of the Teotihuacan period. The relatively low number of sites considered to have definitely undergone construction during the Metepec phase is notable, but bear in mind that nearly half of all DF9 units were coded "insufficient evidence for judgment" on this data field.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Midden deposits on site. At the outset of the TMP it was hoped that stratified middens could be found that would be strategic for excavations that could help refine the ceramic chronology. Disappointingly, very little evidence of such middens was visible on the surface and only 11 possible or definite middens are coded in DF9 (Figure 3.x). It seems likely that most midden material was recycled for use in later structures. There were a few exceptions, such as a midden deposit in site 39:N6W3 into which TMP excavation E12 was dug. The excavation spot is actually in the part of 39:N6W3 that is in sector N6W4 (Millon et al. 1973:6). Some other TMP excavations encountered deep layers of refuse, such as E23, in the Tepantitla apartment compound, 1:N4E2 (Millon 1992:346-47, Fig. 2).

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: Quantity of "lajas" observed. Lajas are tabular building stones used for a variety of purposes at Teotihuacan, including the construction of talud-tablero facades.
DF8Metadata_Text: Materials indicative of ancient building activity
DF9Metadata_VarText: Lajas. These naturally tabular stone fragments (probably from some not far distant source) are readily distinguished from ordinary rocks, and should be good indicators of the former present of talud-tablero platform or pyramid facings, since they were used extensively to support the overhanging parts of tableros. A few were used for other purposes, such as flagstones or bases or covers for cysts (e.g., Cache 1 at Tlamimilolpa [Linné 1942:121, 142]). They were present in varying quantities on the surface of 3,726 cases (Figure 3.x), supporting our impression that talud-tablero features were very common in Teotihuacan-period substantial structures of all kinds. Lajas reworked by crude flaking along one edge to serve as choppers are counted separately, as data field 142.

Tepetate is the sterile volcanic bedrock that characteristically underlies surface sediments at Teotihuacan, but is also exposed on the surface in many areas. Tepetate was often used as a building material by the prehispanic peoples of this area.
DF8Metadata_Text: Materials indicative of ancient building activity
DF9Metadata_VarText: Tepetate.  Tepetate is the local name for indurated volcanic ash subsoil. Chunks of tepetate were often used as part of the rubble cores of Teotihuacan-period walls. In places the subsoil has been exposed by erosion, but this data field refers to loose fragments of tepetate blocks, often quite small and irregular, which are another good surface indicator of ancient substantial construction. They were observed in varying amounts in 2,560 DF9 cases (Figure 3.x).

DF8Metadata_Text: Materials indicative of ancient building activity
DF9Metadata_VarText: Adobe. Traces of adobes were observed in only 58 cases (Figure 3.x), probably because adobes disintegrate so readily when exposed to rain. Although structures composed mainly of adobes were probably rare at Teotihuacan, adobes are among the materials used for wall cores in apartment compounds and they are often one of the components in the fill of large pyramids and platforms, such as the Moon Pyramid (Cabrera and Sugiyama 1999) and the great surrounding platforms of the Ciudadela (Cabrera et al. 1982:17-18).

DF9Metadata_VarText: Concrete fragments. In the process of decay, Teotihuacan concrete facings of walls and floors often break up into loose chunks, before disintegrating altogether into cascajo and more ephemeral components (usually calcareous but sometimes mud or sand). DF9Metadata_VarText: Unpainted plaster fragments. Teotihuacan walls and floors usually had a layer of whitish calcareous plaster a few millimeters thick applied over their concrete facings. DF9Metadata_VarText: Painted plaster fragments. Sometimes the plaster facings of Teotihuacan walls or floors were painted, at least in part (Figure 3.x). Although the color is not recorded in DF9, it is likely that the vast majority of the 422 cases were red, since this is by far the most common color in excavated structures. Sites with traces of painted plaster suggest the possible presence of mural paintings. However, there are numerous excavated cases in which simple red borders were added to otherwise plain white plaster surfaces. Data field 34 records evidence of murals in situ.

accdbMetadata_VarDescription_Long: Counts of "almena" fragments collected. Almenas are a type of roof decoration, typically made of stone, but also made of pottery, particularly granular ware.
DF8Metadata_Text: Number of almena fragments collected. Var.28 belongs logically with vars.127-284 — counts of items collected. DF8 shows 661 almena fragments from 384 different sites.
DF9Metadata_VarText: Number of almena fragments collected. Almenas are ornaments that border roofs of many Teotihuacan structures (Figure 3.x). Some of the larger ones are of stone, but most are ceramic. Macroscopically they appear to be made of Granular Ware, a fabric used for large jars or amphoras, shown clearly by instrumental neutron activation studies to be foreign to Teotihuacan, perhaps from a source in Guerrero (Cowgill and Neff 2001). I do not know whether any compositional studies have confirmed that almenas are actually made of the same ware, although macroscopic examination suggests it. A total of 661 almena fragments from 384 sites were collected by the TMP (Figure 3.x). Highest numbers were collected from sites 38:N3W1 (22), 16S:N2W1 (19), and 62:N5W3 (13). Unusual numbers of almena fragments were collected from sites in sector N3W1, totaling more than 137 (21% of the total of 661). In general almenas were fairly numerous elsewhere west of the Avenue of the Dead, in the W1 to W3 columns and rows N1 to N6. Only a few were collected from further west and surprisingly few were found more than 500 m east of the Avenue of the Dead. Most were associated with apartment compounds, and presumably their abundance has some relationship to socioeconomic statuses of neighborhoods. (We should try to figure out how much of the pattern might be due to different propensities of field crews to collect almenas).

accdbMetadata_Comments: The intent of this field was to gather information pertaining to the deliberate destruction by fire of much of Teotihuacan late in its Classic Period history; presumably, an attempt was made to record evidence for burning at a scale compatible with such an event, and not related to cooking, pottery firing, or similarly mundane activities.
DF8Metadata_Text: Evidence of burned ancient structure. In 1979, a total of 212 sites were coded 1, 2, or 3. However, this does not include much of the additional evidence for burning that was collected in surveys by Pedro Baños addressed to this particular point in the late 70s or early 80s. Much of this new evidence has probably never been added to DF8, hence this variable **MISSES A LOT OF CASES!**
DF9Metadata_VarText: Evidence of burned ancient structure. This data field is of particular interest because excavated Teotihuacan-period structures sometimes show evidence of destruction by fire, and the extent of fiery destruction has implications for the circumstances surrounding the end of the city. In DF9, evidence of burning was noted for only 212 cases (Figure 3.x). However, at Millon's direction, Baños resurveyed large parts of the city in the late 70s or early 80s, and found much additional evidence of burning, much of which has not been added to DF9. It appears that burning was widespread among the temples and palaces in the central part of the city, but much less prevalent elsewhere, where it seems more likely that Teotihuacan Period structures were often abandoned and left to decay (e.g., Techinantitla) or briefly abandoned and then reoccupied by people making ceramics in the Coyotlatelco tradition (e.g., site __:N1E7 in the Metepec Hacienda area [Rattray 1983, 1987]). (We need to look up more data from the Baños survey. Copies of his records should be in GC's possession at ASU. DF8Metadata_Text: Ancient architectural features in place
DF9Metadata_VarText: Murals. Traces of in situ murals were recorded in 45 cases (Figure 3.x). Many of these may be from excavated structures. Excavations would surely reveal more murals in sites where no traces were visible on the surface, but the prevalence of murals in Teotihuacan apartment compounds is still a matter of debate. It seems unlikely that there were many in residences occupied by people of low status or little wealth. Most surviving murals are on interior walls, because they were more protected there. A few murals in good condition survive on exterior walls, such as on the Avenue of the Dead in the "Puma" Group (Millon 1973: Fig. 10b). [Also shown in Miller 1973 and/or de la Fuente 1995?] Very faded but unmistakable murals are visible on some pyramid exteriors, such as the "Adosada" platform attached to the Feathered Serpent Pyramid in the Ciudadela. There is little doubt that at least the central parts of Teotihuacan were very colorful. [[Data fields 30-37:  Ancient architectural features found in situ. DF9Metadata_VarText: Primary architectural interpretation of site during the Patlachique-Tzacualli phase
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Primary architectural interpretation of site. We felt that trying to code the type of structure and what we thought it was used for tended to conflate two different things, so we set up data fields 44-47 to refer strictly to what kind of a structure it was thought to have been, and data fields 53-56 to refer to what we thought it was used for. [Refer to Hopkins 1987 "network" paper in McClung & Rattray 1987]  Because of frequent ambiguities in interpretations, we set up data fields 48-51 to refer to alternative architectural interpretations and data fields 57-60 to refer to alternative functional interpretations. We did not feel that our chronological control was often sufficient to make distinctions among specific ceramic phases, so we lumped them into time spans covering two or more phases. There is a great deal of ceramic evidence for pre-Miccaotli (i.e., Patlachique and/or Tzacualli, very rarely also Cuanalan phase) occupation at or near the sites of later structures but virtually no evidence about pre-Miccaotli structures in terms of their architectural features or likely uses. Any inferences about Miccaotli-Tlamimilolpa phase structures or uses simply assume that they were the same as in the Xolalpan-Metepec phases, except in rare cases where there did not seem to have been a post-Tlamimilolpa occupation. Very few, if any, structures were judged to date to the Oxtoticpac phase and, as of 2002, the very existence of an identifiable Oxtoticpac phase within the city of Teotihuacan was in question. For these reasons, DATA FIELDS 44, 45, 47, 48, 49, 51, 53, 54, 56, 57, 58, and 60 ARE OF EXTREMELY LIMITED OR NO VALUE. [Just get rid of them in the version for distribution, and simplify the discussion?]

DF9Metadata_VarText: Primary functional interpretation of site during the Xolalpan-Metepec interval. Among categories considered fairly meaningful by Cowgill, the most abundant are: intermediate status residence (1,860), high status residence (275), low status residence (546), residence of uncertain status (127), temple platform (215), platform of probable religious significance (254), plaza (354), and "unoccupied in this interval" (574). Figures 3.x to 3.x show these categories. The category "intermediate status residence" is probably over-represented and "low status residence" and "high status residence" are probably under-represented. It must be emphasized that status judgments are very rarely based on any differences in proportions of fine ceramics or other materials likely to have been costly that were large enough to have been apparent during the surface survey. Excavations and statistical analyses of surface collections will improve these initial status judgments. The breakdown into many categories of temples is probably over-fine for many purposes, but is pretty clear that below the Sun, Moon, and Feathered Serpent Pyramids there are at least two or three levels of free-standing temples, in addition to the fact that many researchers call the platforms within apartment compounds "temples." Rather than trying to tease these levels out of the DF9 codings, however, it would be better to work with the lists prepared by Cowgill and Millon in early 1981. (Locate these lists! Possibly include as a new data field in one of the electronic files.) In general, data field 55 codings for workshops should be ignored. Many real workshops were probably missed in this coding and a number of those coded as workshops may well not be. For category 24 of data field 55, "obsidian workshop," data fields 285 and 286 are preferable. For category 25, "pottery workshop," data field 287 is much preferable. Category 42, "residential workshop," is also very dubious. Even data fields 285-287, however, should be used with extreme caution, since the job of trying to securely identify workshops at Teotihuacan is still in process, and in most cases will require reexaminations of collections, revisiting sites in the field, and/or new excavations.

DF10Metadata_Text: Sometimes two or more distinct architectural units, separate cases in DF9, are clearly parts of some larger architectural entity that can safely be assumed to have been culturally significant to the Teotihuacanos. These are called "complexes." A three-pyramid complex, such as Plaza One (1:N5W2) is a good example. Rarely, many distinct structures seem linked in a spatially very large but fairly well-defined association. These are called "macrocomplexes" in DF9. An example is the "Avenue of the Dead" macrocomplex. A macrocomplex can include no complexes or one or more complexes as sub-units, plus any number of individual sites. However, every complex should be either wholly within one macrocomplex or wholly outside – it does not make sense for a complex to be partly within and partly outside a macrocomplex. Nothing whatever about complexes or macrocomplexes appears explicitly on the SSR. Some information of this kind was written on SSRs in SSR fields 9 (location in relation to other sites), 10 (description of site), and/or 30 (comments). However, this varied greatly among field crews. Much of the interpretation of complexes and macrocomplexes was made after Millon had completed the "interpretations" sheets published in Millon et al. (1973). Many complexes are very clear but, even in the case of three-pyramid complexes, there is often uncertainty about exactly which very nearby structures should be included or excluded, and there are even more problems in deciding which sites on the edges of macrocomplexes belong within the macrocomplex. In many cases judgments may have been made initially by those filling out the code sheets, but eventually all were checked and revised by Cowgill. Nevertheless, some uncertain judgments had to be made. Investigations regarding complexes and macrocomplexes should be carried out with careful reference to the data in Millon et al. (1973) and, if possible, the SSRs. The key data fields for identifying DF9 cases assigned to the same complex are 80 and 81. Data field 81 is the four-character label of the sector within which all or most of the complex lies, and data field 80 is a numerical designation for the complexes within each sector. Thus, complex 3:N5W3 would be the third complex among complexes located mainly within sector N5W3. All cases assigned to the same complex have the same ID for data fields 80 and 81, even if the case lies in a different map sector. For cases not assigned to any complex (which are the great majority of cases), data field 80 was coded "missing data or inapplicable" and data field 81 was coded "XXXX." Data fields 82 and 83 work the same way for macrocomplexes. This whole system is a rather cumbersome way for introducing two levels of case groupings above the basic DF9 level, while maintaining a simple "flat file" structure. In DF9, data fields 61-79 repeat the same information for each case in the same complex (except for errors, to which this system was especially prone), and data fields 84-89 repeat the same information for each case in the same macrocomplex. Today, complexes and macrocomplexes could be handled much better by a relational database approach in which separate files for complexes and macrocomplexes were linked to the file for individual sites.As is the case for architectural and functional interpretations of individual sites, data fields characterizing complexes and macrocomplexes for intervals other than Xolalpan-Metepec are of very limited value and should generally be ignored. Data field 63 (observable character of complex in the Xolalpan-Metepec interval) is perhaps most useful for identifying cases belonging to three-pyramid complexes, although some of the other codings are somewhat useful. In general, other data fields for characterizing even Xolalpan-Metepec complexes and macrocomplexes do not seem terribly useful.;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;

DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Sometimes two or more distinct architectural units, separate cases in DF9, are clearly parts of some larger architectural entity that can safely be assumed to have been culturally significant to the Teotihuacanos. These are called "complexes." A three-pyramid complex, such as Plaza One (1:N5W2) is a good example. Rarely, many distinct structures seem linked in a spatially very large but fairly well-defined association. These are called "macrocomplexes" in DF9. An example is the "Avenue of the Dead" macrocomplex. A macrocomplex can include no complexes or one or more complexes as sub-units, plus any number of individual sites. However, every complex should be either wholly within one macrocomplex or wholly outside – it does not make sense for a complex to be partly within and partly outside a macrocomplex. Nothing whatever about complexes or macrocomplexes appears explicitly on the SSR. Some information of this kind was written on SSRs in SSR fields 9 (location in relation to other sites), 10 (description of site), and/or 30 (comments). However, this varied greatly among field crews. Much of the interpretation of complexes and macrocomplexes was made after Millon had completed the "interpretations" sheets published in Millon et al. (1973). Many complexes are very clear but, even in the case of three-pyramid complexes, there is often uncertainty about exactly which very nearby structures should be included or excluded, and there are even more problems in deciding which sites on the edges of macrocomplexes belong within the macrocomplex. In many cases judgments may have been made initially by those filling out the code sheets, but eventually all were checked and revised by Cowgill. Nevertheless, some uncertain judgments had to be made. Investigations regarding complexes and macrocomplexes should be carried out with careful reference to the data in Millon et al. (1973) and, if possible, the SSRs. The key data fields for identifying DF9 cases assigned to the same complex are 80 and 81. Data field 81 is the four-character label of the sector within which all or most of the complex lies, and data field 80 is a numerical designation for the complexes within each sector. Thus, complex 3:N5W3 would be the third complex among complexes located mainly within sector N5W3. All cases assigned to the same complex have the same ID for data fields 80 and 81, even if the case lies in a different map sector. For cases not assigned to any complex (which are the great majority of cases), data field 80 was coded "missing data or inapplicable" and data field 81 was coded "XXXX." Data fields 82 and 83 work the same way for macrocomplexes. This whole system is a rather cumbersome way for introducing two levels of case groupings above the basic DF9 level, while maintaining a simple "flat file" structure. In DF9, data fields 61-79 repeat the same information for each case in the same complex (except for errors, to which this system was especially prone), and data fields 84-89 repeat the same information for each case in the same macrocomplex. Today, complexes and macrocomplexes could be handled much better by a relational database approach in which separate files for complexes and macrocomplexes were linked to the file for individual sites.As is the case for architectural and functional interpretations of individual sites, data fields characterizing complexes and macrocomplexes for intervals other than Xolalpan-Metepec are of very limited value and should generally be ignored. Data field 63 (observable character of complex in the Xolalpan-Metepec interval) is perhaps most useful for identifying cases belonging to three-pyramid complexes, although some of the other codings are somewhat useful. In general, other data fields for characterizing even Xolalpan-Metepec complexes and macrocomplexes do not seem terribly useful.;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;

Rarely, many distinct structures seem linked in a spatially very large but fairly well-defined association. These are called "macrocomplexes" in DF9. An example is the "Avenue of the Dead" macrocomplex. A macrocomplex can include no complexes or one or more complexes as sub-units, plus any number of individual sites. However, every complex should be either wholly within one macrocomplex or wholly outside – it does not make sense for a complex to be partly within and partly outside a macrocomplex. Nothing whatever about complexes or macrocomplexes appears explicitly on the SSR. Some information of this kind was written on SSRs in SSR fields 9 (location in relation to other sites), 10 (description of site), and/or 30 (comments). However, this varied greatly among field crews. Much of the interpretation of complexes and macrocomplexes was made after Millon had completed the "interpretations" sheets published in Millon et al. (1973). Many complexes are very clear but, even in the case of three-pyramid complexes, there is often uncertainty about exactly which very nearby structures should be included or excluded, and there are even more problems in deciding which sites on the edges of macrocomplexes belong within the macrocomplex. In many cases judgments may have been made initially by those filling out the code sheets, but eventually all were checked and revised by Cowgill. Nevertheless, some uncertain judgments had to be made. Investigations regarding complexes and macrocomplexes should be carried out with careful reference to the data in Millon et al. (1973) and, if possible, the SSRs. The key data fields for identifying DF9 cases assigned to the same complex are 80 and 81. Data field 81 is the four-character label of the sector within which all or most of the complex lies, and data field 80 is a numerical designation for the complexes within each sector. Thus, complex 3:N5W3 would be the third complex among complexes located mainly within sector N5W3. All cases assigned to the same complex have the same ID for data fields 80 and 81, even if the case lies in a different map sector. For cases not assigned to any complex (which are the great majority of cases), data field 80 was coded "missing data or inapplicable" and data field 81 was coded "XXXX." Data fields 82 and 83 work the same way for macrocomplexes. This whole system is a rather cumbersome way for introducing two levels of case groupings above the basic DF9 level, while maintaining a simple "flat file" structure. In DF9, data fields 61-79 repeat the same information for each case in the same complex (except for errors, to which this system was especially prone), and data fields 84-89 repeat the same information for each case in the same macrocomplex. Today, complexes and macrocomplexes could be handled much better by a relational database approach in which separate files for complexes and macrocomplexes were linked to the file for individual sites.As is the case for architectural and functional interpretations of individual sites, data fields characterizing complexes and macrocomplexes for intervals other than Xolalpan-Metepec are of very limited value and should generally be ignored. Data field 63 (observable character of complex in the Xolalpan-Metepec interval) is perhaps most useful for identifying cases belonging to three-pyramid complexes, although some of the other codings are somewhat useful. In general, other data fields for characterizing even Xolalpan-Metepec complexes and macrocomplexes do not seem terribly useful.;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;

DF9Metadata_VarText: Prehispanic wells in site. Millon (1973:__) discusses the effort to locate prehispanic wells. At least until very recently, the water table in most of Teotihuacan was only a few meters below ground level – well within the depth that could be dug into the tepetate subsoil with the technology available to Teotihuacanos. In fact, the springs and marshy area in and around sectors S1W4 and S1W5 and extending to the southwest are essentially where the water table reached the level of the ground surface. In several cases, these wells, typically circular and somewhat more than a meter in diameter, with footholds cut at intervals into their sides, were found sealed under Teotihuacan-period floors. In other cases, it may be less certain that they are not post-Teotihuacan in origin, and some Teotihuacan wells may have continued in use up to recent times. They are coded as present or possibly present in 24 DF9 cases (Figure 3.x). Millon and Cowgill suspect that many more Teotihuacan wells existed than were located by the TMP survey. These wells are important evidence of one source of water for the Teotihuacanos, especially during the dry season.

DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Vegetation cover at the time the collection was made. These data fields are important for information about land use in the 1960s and, especially, for information bearing on the ease or difficulty of spotting objects during surface survey. Milpa (maize field), barley, beans, cut alfalfa, uncut alfalfa, nopales, fallow land, and uncultivated are all explicit categories on the SSR, while magueyes, if present, were routinely noted in the "other vegetation" space on the SSR. "Fallow" refers to cases where no crop was growing at the time of survey but there was evidence that the tract had been cultivated in the recent past. "Uncultivated" refers to land that may have been cultivated in the remote past, but not recently. Collections from uncut alfalfa were particularly difficult to make because of the very dense ground cover, and cut alfalfa was only slightly less difficult. Moreover, alfalfa fields have often been leveled (data field 112) to make irrigation possible, in the process destroying ancient mounds and other features. Mature barley also made collection difficult. Uncultivated tracts also often yielded sparse collections, partly because many were covered with grass and partly because they did not have the benefit of recent plowing, which tends to bring objects to the surface. Closely-planted nopal orchards offered challenges to surveyors but the ground surface was often not greatly obscured. Magueyes leave the ground quite open and the pits for planting magueyes may bring up material from some depth. Quite often more than one type of vegetation was noted for a single case. If one type was noted as present but the extent not recorded, and all other types present at all were noted present only in a small or moderate proportion of the site or only scattered across the site, it is likely that the type recorded merely as "present" was the dominant type on that site

DF9Metadata_VarText: Cut Alfalfa Alfalfa cut at the time of survey was found on part or all of 94 DF9 units, and uncut alfalfa on 162 units. As can be seen in Figure 3.x, most alfalfa, which is highly dependent on irrigation, was concentrated in an area of about 2000 by 2000 m, running from the N2 to the S2 row and the W4 to W1 column. Much of the irrigation water for alfalfa comes from deep drilled wells. Another district with considerable alfalfa was in the same north-south rows, from E3 to E4, and extending into sectors S1E5 and S1E6. Alfalfa fields in southwestern sectors S2W8 and S2W7 were probably watered by canals from the permanent springs in and near S1W4. There were also a number of alfalfa fields in far southern sectors S5W1 and S5E1.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Magueyes. Magueyes (century plants, genus Agave) were being grown on part of all of 753 DF9 units (Figure 3.x). These are especially important today, as in the past, because their fermented sap produces pulque, a nutritious and mildly alcoholic beverage. Their leaves are an important source of fiber, coarser than cotton, that can be spun and then used for netting or woven into textiles. The tough layer just under the surface of the leaves may have been used for paper. The leaves themselves can be used as building material and for fuel. For more information about maguey use, see especially Parsons and Parsons (1990).

Milpa (maize field), barley, beans, cut alfalfa, uncut alfalfa, nopales, fallow land, and uncultivated are all explicit categories on the SSR, while magueyes, if present, were routinely noted in the "other vegetation" space on the SSR. "Fallow" refers to cases where no crop was growing at the time of survey but there was evidence that the tract had been cultivated in the recent past. "Uncultivated" refers to land that may have been cultivated in the remote past, but not recently. Collections from uncut alfalfa were particularly difficult to make because of the very dense ground cover, and cut alfalfa was only slightly less difficult. Moreover, alfalfa fields have often been leveled (data field 112) to make irrigation possible, in the process destroying ancient mounds and other features. Mature barley also made collection difficult. Uncultivated tracts also often yielded sparse collections, partly because many were covered with grass and partly because they did not have the benefit of recent plowing, which tends to bring objects to the surface. Closely-planted nopal orchards offered challenges to surveyors but the ground surface was often not greatly obscured. Magueyes leave the ground quite open and the pits for planting magueyes may bring up material from some depth. Quite often more than one type of vegetation was noted for a single case. If one type was noted as present but the extent not recorded, and all other types present at all were noted present only in a small or moderate proportion of the site or only scattered across the site, it is likely that the type recorded merely as "present" was the dominant type on that site

DF9Metadata_VarText: Type of water for crops at the time of the survey. The four categories for this data field derive directly from the SSR, so they were routinely reported (Figure 3.x). Humedad (138 cases) refers to naturally moist land, essentially limited to the area of chinampa-like cultivation in the southwest part of the survey area (check!). Temporal (3,822 cases) refers to dry farming. Riego (used if any part of the site was in riego, 366 cases) refers to irrigation, using water supplied by canals or pumps. DF9Metadata_VarText: Status of plowing when the collection was made. Plowing, with the relatively shallow plows in use at the time of the TMP survey, disturbs the upper 15-20 cm or so of sites, brings much material to the surface, and kills much of the ground cover, facilitating the making of relatively large collections. Plowing followed by rain increases visibility of objects even more. This was probably the case for most of the 1,868 DF9 cases coded as plowed but not freshly plowed. Only in 11 cases was part or all of the site freshly plowed at the time the collection was made. There were 435 sites coded as probably plowed in the past but not recently (Figure 3.x). Among the 2,429 coded as probably never plowed, many may have been plowed at some time in the remote past, although those on steeper ground were probably never plowed at all. Upon excavation, it is not uncommon to see plow marks on the latest well-preserved floors, and even shallow plowing has often destroyed the very latest floors (often but not always post-Teotihuacan).

DF8Metadata_Text: General slope of site setting
DF9Metadata_VarText: General slope of site setting. Cowgill is no longer sure whether much effort was made to standardize the use of terms like "slight," "moderate," and "considerable" for this data field. No DF9 cases were coded as occurring on very steep slopes, which is quite accurate according to Cowgill's concept of what counts as "very steep." Many sites in Mesoamerica are situated in far more rugged topography than any that occurs within the urban zone of Teotihuacan, most of which is in the range from flat to moderately sloping, with the steepest contexts being in the northwest, on the slopes of Cerros Colorado and Malinalco. In the far south, the land begins to slope upward toward Cerro Patlachique. In the final codings for this data field, some use may have been made of the contours on the field data sheets. DF9Metadata_VarText: "Plastersmoothers." 4,240 (Figure 3.x). Most "plastersmoothers" are objects of porous lava with a tabular body and a knob handle (Figure 3.x), suitable for some kind of abrading but singularly ill-suited for spreading or smoothing plaster. A few "plastersmoothers" are objects of denser stone, often with loop handles, (Figure 3.x) that probably had a different use and seem somewhat more likely to have been employed in the building industry. All, or nearly all "plastersmoothers" pertain to the Teotihuacan Period.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Fire gods (Huehueteotls). 33 (Figure 3.x and 3.x). These stone figures of a bent old man with fangs, seated cross-legged and with a bowl on the head, are frequently found in excavations of Teotihuacan apartment compounds, often near the altar in a central courtyard. They are likely associated with ritual at the apartment compound level, involving the multiple households of the compound but probably not groups outside the compound. That is, they are probably an element in the ideational basis for corporate aspects of compounds. Umberger (1987) and López Luján (1989) discuss an interesting Aztec copy and partial reinterpretation of the form.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Total obsidian
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Obsidian category counts.  DF9 records a total of over 230,293 obsidian objects, of which the most abundant categories are waste, prismatic blades, scrapers, bifacial points/knives, and polyhedral cores. Regrettably and, in retrospect, quite oddly,  the SSRs and DF9 do not include distinctions between green obsidian (mostly from the Cerro de las Navajas source near Pachuca, about 55 km away), gray obsidian (nearly all from the nearby source near Otumba), and any unusual obsidian that might be from other sources. Tabulations making these distinction may exist in the possession of Michael Spence (ask him!). Some other obsidian data missing from earlier versions of DF8 and DF9 was provided by Spence in 1982. Unfortunately, the existing obsidian counts in DF9 are a mix of counts of categories as defined by Spence as of 1982 and tabulations based on category definitions used by various TMP personnel earlier, and it is not easy (impossible?) to tell which criteria are represented in specific DF9 cases. Personal communications from Spence suggest the following: (1) Data fields 151 and 153 ("points" and "knives") are probably best thought of as a combined "bifacial" category (total 16,724, Figure 3.x), because the point/knife distinction is probably not very accurately reflected in DF9 counts. Spence tends to put more bifaces under "knives" than the field crews did. (2) The counts for total obsidian (data field 147, Figure 3.x), prismatic blades (data field 148, 72,351, Figure 3.x)), bifacials (points plus knives), and polyhedral cores (data field 152, 8,598, Figure 3.x) are probably pretty good. (3) Spence feels that field crews tended to miss quite a few scrapers (data field 150, 29,390, Figure 3.x) and put them into "waste" (data field 149, 89,427, Figure 3.x). This is particularly true of what Spence calls "amorphous scrapers." (4) Some prismatic blades were also missed by field crews and counted as "waste" and so were many nodule fragments (data field 157, 2,931, Figure 3.x). Cowgill believes that Spence counts anything still showing some outer cortex under "nodules" rather than "waste." (5) Utilized flakes were handled erratically in the field analyses, and this makes data field 156 pretty useless. Data field 154 (eccentrics, including figurines, 99, Figure 3.x) is probably pretty good, although coders may have missed some cases in going from the SSRs to the code sheets. All the above remarks apply to the success with which DF9 captures the information in the collections actually made by field crews. A separate issue is the extent to which different field crews had differing tendencies to make large or small obsidian collections and the extent to which they collected abundant but perhaps less interesting categories, such as "waste." [Spence may have data bearing on these issues.]

DF8Metadata_Text: Total figurines. **Total figurines and "puppet" fragments are OK**, but the rest of the DF8 figurine data is so incomplete that it **SHOULD NOT BE USED AT ALL**.
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Ceramic figurine counts. A total of 44,701 figurine fragments are recorded in DF9 (Figure 3.x). This total count is quite reliable, although occasionally analysts misclassified some fragments of other modeled objects as figurines, or the reverse. Fragments of jointed or "puppet" figurines (data field 181) were also readily recognized (total 4,892, Figure 3.x). However, virtually no data on figurines by phase were available for the creation of DF9 and data fields 172-180, figurine counts by phase, must be ignored. Data field 171 (figurine heads) is also not useful. Collections with exceptionally high numbers of figurine fragments are those from sites 4:N2E5 (341), 60`:N1E5 (264), and 5:N2E5 (262). These are all, however, from sites where exceptionally intensive collections were made, so these extreme numbers should be somewhat discounted. Perhaps more significant are sites such as 23:N5W3 (235) (now known as Cosotlan 23, where Kristin Sullivan has made an intensive surface collection [Sullivan 2007]), 79:N6W2 (176), 14:N5W3 (171) and 20W:N3E1 (136). These are among sites that might be compared with data field 288, which tabulates sites identified by Warren Barbour as having notable figurine concentrations. Sites with exceptionally high proportions of total figurines relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec sherds plus Thin Orange, where the denominator is 20 or more, are 74:N6W2 (60/37), 7:N5W3 (64/71), L18:N7E1 (35/46), and 37:N4W2 (28/40). These ratios should be treated with caution, because some cases may include considerable numbers of pre-Miccaotli or post-Metepec figurines, perhaps especially Aztec. Collections with unusually high proportions of "puppet" fragments relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec sherds plus Thin Orange are from 7:N5W3 (13/71), 66:N4E2 (7/57), 8:N6E1 (2/20), 46:N2W6 (2/22), and 43N:N1E5 (7/78). (None of these have yet had the benefit of Bayesian or other smoothing techniques.) Far more extensive tabulations of TMP figurines, by types, body parts, and attributes, as well as phases, were made by Dr. Kim Goldsmith in the 1980s. Sets of these paper records are in the Teotihuacan Archaeological Research Center and in Cowgill's possession at ASU. After unsatisfactory efforts to create an electronic file using an Apple II-E computer, these records have been entered by Kristin Sullivan and Janet Montoya into an Access database at ASU. This file will be an important addition to the data in the files we describe here [What is its name? Where can it be found?]. Especially important publications on Teotihuacan Period and later figurines include Barbour (1976, 1987, 1998), Goldsmith (2000), Scott (1982, 1993, 2001), and Montoya (____).

DF8Metadata_Text: Total Candeleros ("Candeleros" abbreviated as "Cdos")
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Candelero fragments.  The TMP collected 15,521 candelero fragments, of which 9,118 were "common" (Figure 3.x) and 6,403 were other kinds (Figure 3.x). Candeleros are small unslipped objects, usually with twin chambers, thought to have been used for burning incense. Data field 194 records total candelero fragments of all types. Data field 200 is the count of so-called "common" candeleros, relatively crude examples with finger-gouging in the soft clay and two chambers (Figure 3.x). Attempts to phase other candelero types for DF9 were largely unsuccessful and data fields 195-199 should be ignored. On the basis of more recent evidence, including excavations at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid in 1988-89, Cowgill doubts if any candeleros were made before the Late Tlamimilolpa phase and thinks that most of them at that time were single-chambered. Some analysts think that "common" candeleros are distinctive of the Metepec phase, but Cowgill thinks that many "common" candeleros may date to Xolalpan and that other types did not necessarily disappear in the Metepec phase. By subtracting data field 200 from data field 194 one can get the count of the quite heterogeneous category of "non-common" candeleros. For more information on Teotihuacan candeleros, see Kolb (1988). A promising study of TMP candeleros by Deborah Cembellin has foundered. It has been carried further by Nawa Sugiyama (20__) but has not yet been integrated with other TMP data files. Figure 3.x illustrates examples of "non-common" candeleros. It is likely that candeleros were a local Teotihuacan invention, beginning as single-chambered objects in the Late Tlamimilolpa phase, then being made of two (rarely more) joined chambers, and, in the Xolalpan and Metepec phases, the great majority were made as single objects in which two chambers were formed. Candeleros do not seem to survive the fall of Teotihuacan. In spite of their simplicity and seeming association with individual rituals, Cowgill suspects that they were somehow connected with the state ideology. When they occur outside the Teotihuacan core area, they are probably one of the best markers of a Teotihuacan connection we have. (More about candeleros abroad, Matacapan, Pacific Guatemala, etc.). Candeleros were recounted during the ceramics reanalyses carried out in the 1970s. However, Cowgill decided not add the data to the Reanalysis file because only the same two categories, total candeleros and "common" candeleros, were recorded, and these are both so obvious that it seemed extremely unlikely that the new counts would differ appreciably from those already in DF9. In retrospect, having this information readily available might have helped to resolve questions about whether exactly the same collections as in DF9 were being reanalyzed in some problematic cases. 	Districts with unusually high ratios of "common" candeleros to total phased Xolalpan-Metepec ceramics, ranging upwards from 12%, include the southern part of sector N1W2 (the northern part of the La Ventilla district), sector N2E3, and, to a lesser extent, much of the Great Compound (sector N1W1) (Figure 3.x). Other more localized high ratios occur in the northeastern part of N6W3, southwestern N2E5, southeastern N1E8, and southwestern S1W1. Unusually high ratios of non-common candeleros to total phased Xolalpan-Metepec ceramics (upwards of 9%) occur in the eastern part of N6W4, the northeastern part of N2E3, southeastern N2W2 and northeastern N1W2, northwestern N1E6, and northwestern S1W3 (Figure 3.x). Relative to total candeleros, "common" ones are especially above average in western N4W1, southeastern N2E2 and northwestern N1E3, southern N1W2, southwestern S1W1, and southern S3W1 (in the Tlajinga district) (Figure 3.x). Non-common candeleros are especially abundant relative to "common" ones in northeastern N6W4, southeastern N5W3 and northeastern N4W3, northwestern N3E4 (the Merchants' Enclave), and northeastern N1E7 (the Hacienda Metepec area) (Figure 3.x).

DF8Metadata_Text: Three-prong burners
DF9Metadata_VarText: Three-prong burners. The TMP collected 5,182 fragments of these objects (Figure 3.x). They are open bowls of Coarse Matte Ware, with flat bottoms, relatively straight outslanting sides, and usually direct undecorated rims. Three hollow prongs are attached to the rim and slant upward and inwardly (Figure 3.x). Sometimes moldmade figures are attached to the prongs (Figure 3.x). Note that the example published by Berrin and Pasztory (1993:248, Figure 129) has been extensively and very clumsily and inaccurately restored [Look for better illos. to cite]. No one could claim that any three-prong burners are objects of great beauty, but they are not the lumpy and asymmetrical monstrosities depicted in this figure. Variants with clear chronological significance have not been recognized, although Cowgill suspects that the form is rare or absent in the earlier part of the Teotihuacan Period. This is curious, if true, because vessels of the same general form, though differing in details, are found in the Middle Preclassic, especially in the Late Cantera phase, ca. 600-500 BC, at Chalcatzingo in the nearby Valley of Morelos, (Grove 1984:78-79, Fig. 20; Cyphers 1987:247, Fig. 13.67) and also at Tres Zapotes in the southern Gulf lowlands (Cyphers 1987:248; Cowgill, personal observation). Body sherds of three-prong burners are often impossible to distinguish from those of the Coarse Matte bowls that formed the bases for Teotihuacan composite censers. However, censer bowls have flanged rims and lack prongs, and since the TMP only collected feature sherds, it is rarely a problem to distinguish three-prong burners from censers in the DF9 material. Three-prong burners sometimes show evidence of burning on the interior. They may have been used to some extent for incense burning in rituals, but they also very likely functioned as utilitarian little stoves. During the winter months it can become very chilly indoors at Teotihuacan, and three-prong burners could have been effective space heaters. It has very often been assumed that other vessels containing food to be cooked or heated were set atop the prongs, but Cowgill has examined hundreds of the prongs without ever seeing one that showed the slightest trace of the abrasion that would be expected if other ceramic objects had been placed atop them. As space heaters, the burners might have been moved from room to room, and handles that stayed relatively cool would have facilitated moving the burners. However, the positions of the prongs make them seem very ill-suited for use as handles. Many, but not all, prongs have perforations at both ends, and it is possible that cords were passed through the prongs so that the vessels could be suspended. It would seem that such cords would be in danger of burning, but perhaps this could have been avoided by restricting the fire to charcoal in the lower part of the vessel. This may be the most plausible interpretation of what is still a puzzling form. Relative to total phased Xolalpan-Metepec ceramics, ratios of three-prong burners were above average (6% and more) in the "Outer Old City" [rename?] (in and near sector N6W3), the southeastern part of N5W3, in N5E2 and N5E3, in N3E5 and N2E5, and in S2W1 (Figure 3.x). It has been suggested that burners, as well as the technologically similar Coarse Matte bowls for composite censers, may have been manufactured in the "Outer Old City," but at present this is only a suggestion. [Ring binder shd be checked for possibly a bit to add; there's a lot more detail noted.]

DF8Metadata_Text: Handled covers
DF9Metadata_VarText: Handled covers (tapaplatos). DF9 includes 6,661 tapaplato fragments. These are plates or very shallow dishes made of Fine Matte Ware  (Figure 3.x). Berrin and Pasztory (1993:248, Fig. 128) show three good examples. Less experienced ceramic analysts sometimes have difficulty distinguishing small rim sherds of handled covers from those of very shallow crudely burnished bowls, and a few cases in DF9 may be misclassified. Many, but not all, have three loop handles attached to the convex side. Set with the convex side down, these loop handles serve as supports, and it is very common to see flat abraded facets on the loops, suggesting that they had been set on hard, flat surfaces. Many have a shallow mold-impressed design on the convex surface (Figure 3.x). These molded designs may prove to have chronological significance, but so far handled covers have not been phased. Excavations in the Feathered Serpent Pyramid indicate that handled covers with loop handles begin to occur at least as early as the Early Tlamimilolpa phase, but various statistical analyses of TMP data repeatedly imply that they were especially associated with the Metepec phase. Cowgill does not believe there is any evidence that they continued to be made in post-Metepec times. Some handled covers show evidence of burning on their concave (interior) surface, and some may show evidence of burning on the convex (exterior) surface. It is likely that at least one of their uses was as censers (Cowgill 1987; Rattray 1987b). Cowgill (1987) considered the possibility that one use may have been as lids over other vessels, "lunch buckets" intended to keep contents warm and fresh, with cords passed through the loop handles to keep them in place, but he judged this unlikely. In some Teotihuacan burials handled covers have in fact been found placed as lids over other vessels (Séjourné 1966:53 and plate 15) but this mortuary usage need not reflect how they were used among the living. Handled covers remain a distinctive and rather enigmatic form apparently strongly associated with Teotihuacan. They were collected in highest proportions (over 10% of total phased Xolalpan-Metepec sherds) in a broad strip along and east of the Avenue of the Dead, from the Moon Pyramid to somewhat south of the Sun Pyramid, and in the Ciudadela (Figure 3.x). Although proportions of handled covers tend to be high in this district, absolute numbers are not great because Xolalpan-Metepec sherds are not abundant in this district, in part because of the great number of restored structures along the Avenue. Proportions are also high in the southeastern part of N3W3, where 123 fragments were collected at 20:N3W3 (29% of the 467 Xolalpan-Metepec sherds collected here). In general, lowest proportions relative to Xolalpan-Metepec are toward the edges of the city. At site 25:S4W1 141 tapaplato fragments were collected, nearly 26% of the 549 phased Xolalpan-Metepec sherds collected from this site. Between 50 and 94 fragments were collected at each of another nine sites. DF8Metadata_Text: Total sherds collected. Var.204 does not include all ceramic categories. It includes all phase totals (vars.205-217), plus the following unphased categories: - Burners (var.201), Handled covers (var.202), Total Thin Orange (var.230), Foreign sherds (var.265), Adornos (var.274), Miniatures (var.275), Copas (var.276), "Matte Ware" (var.277), and Disks (var.284). It does **not** include figurines, whorls, seals & stamps, whistles, flutes, earspools, and candeleros.
DF9Metadata_VarText: Total sherds collected. This includes all phased sherds plus most unphased ceramic categories, including three-prong burners (data field 201), tapaplatos (202), total Thin Orange (230), foreign (265), censer or vase ornaments (274), miniatures (275), copas (276), unphased Matte Ware (277), and disks (284). For all DF9 units, total sherds collected sums to 832,974. For some reason, probably because they do not come from vessels, several ceramic categories were not included in data field 204 counts. These are figurines (data field 170), whorls (182), seals and stamps (183), earspools (184), whistles (185), flutes (186), and candeleros (194). When these are added, the grand total of ceramic objects collected by the TMP surface survey is 893,817. This omits some collections, mainly made in 1962, that could not be related in any simple way to DF9 cases, including some that were outside the area covered by the maps in Millon et al. (1973). We should explain that Rattray (2001) divides most locally-made ceramics into several wares: Coarse Matte, Fine Matte, Burnished, Polished Monochrome, Copa (and Copoid), Painted, and San Martín Orange. In fact, however, she has sorted mainly according to forms. In general, each ware has a distinct repertoire of forms, so that any particular form occurs in only one ware. Burnished Ware is mostly ollas and other utilitarian forms, while Polished Ware forms are more likely for serving food and other non-utilitarian purposes. However, in the case of Burnished and Polished Wares, there is actually a continuum of quality of finish, ranging from rather poorly burnished to a very fine polish in which tool marks are scarcely visible. This is partially recognized by categories or adjectives such as "low burnished," "low polished," "pattern polished," and so on. However, one should recognize that a well-defined shape category such as "polished outcurving bowl" (data fields 461-465) includes examples ranging from very finely polished examples to those more accurately described as well burnished. Also, the category "Painted Ware" does not consist of a distinctive repertoire of shapes, but instead reflects the presence of a particular kind of decorative mode on vessels that would otherwise be included in the "Polished Ware" category.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Cuanalan Phase (Ticoman).  Figure 3.x. There is clear evidence of significant Late Preclassic settlements within the TMP survey area, reported summarily and somewhat inaccurately by Sanders et al. (1979), and there are other substantial settlements of this period within the Teotihuacan Valley, notably the type site of Cuanalan (refs, including Manzanilla). Cuanalan is the local variant of what Vaillant (1931) calls Ticoman. Our analyses did not break Cuanalan phase ceramics down by subphases, but probably the majority correspond to Late Ticoman, probably ca. 300-150 B.C. The DF9 total for this phase is 2,736, although a few of these are probably later. By far the largest settlement of this period in the TMP survey area is centered on sector S1W6, where a large village, covering 15 to 30 ha, with perhaps a thousand or more occupants, was located on the nearest well-drained land to the marshy area fed by perennial springs. Today, this is an area of wetland agriculture, with drained fields, in the Puxtla barrio of the municipio of San Juan. Gamboa (2000) reports evidence of wetland practices here as early as Late Tlamimilolpa. However, the proximity of the Cuanalan phase settlement to the marshy area suggests that wetland agriculture may already have been important at that time. If so, this, rather than any special religious or other significance, may have been a major reason for the location of the large Cuanalan village. A much smaller village, not reported by Sanders et al. (1979), covers 6-9 ha and is located in the northeastern part of sector S3E6. There are very sparse scatters of Cuanalan phase ceramics elsewhere within the TMP survey area. However, re-examination of collections by Cowgill suggests that many of the supposed Cuanalan sherds in the apparent weak concentrations in an earlier map (Cowgill 1974:379), especially in sectors N4W7, N4W6, N4W5, N6W4, and N5W2, are probably later. That map remains quite accurate for the large and small villages mentioned above, but is superseded by Figure 3.x. Cuanalan ceramics also occur in the zone just northwest of the area covered by the 1963-70 TMP survey, including the site of Tlachinolpan in sector N7W8 (Blucher 1971) and in N6W6 and N5W6. These revisions in our ideas about the spatial distribution of Cuanalan phase ceramics strengthen the evidence for spatial discontinuities between Cuanalan phase settlements and those of the following Patlachique phase. The map published by Cowgill (1974:379) shows a modest Cuanalan sherd concentration in the region with high Patlachique phase sherd density, in and near map sector N5W2, but Cowgill's later reexamination of these collections found that most or all of the supposed Cuanalan sherds in this area were misidentified. Thus, the Cuanalan settlements do not look like nuclei from which the Patlachique phase settlement developed. Whether or not the Patlachique phase occupants were newcomers, this marked discontinuity in settlement implies a radical change in the nature of the community. (Look up Cowgill 1992b and Blucher 1971 for more info. Also, do the DF9 Cuan counts reflect any of the restudies of collections done by Cowgill in the 1980s? Are these restudies reflected in the REANS file?)

DF9Metadata_VarText: Tezoyuca Phase.  (No map). Only 69 sherds thought to belong to this still poorly-understood complex were identified in the ceramic analyses on which DF9 is based. Of these, 17 are from site 24:N1W6, which is in the northern part of the large Cuanalan phase village, and 13 are from L2:N7E2, far to the northeast, in the present municipality of San Martín de las Pirámides. Six to two sherds were tabulated as Tezoyuca in another nine sites, and single sherds from six more sites in widely scattered parts of the TMP survey area.  It remains to be seen how many of these are correctly identified and whether any significant number of Tezoyuca-complex sherds were unrecognized in other TMP collections. On present evidence, Tezoyuca material seems extremely scarce at Teotihuacan. The Tezoyuca phase is better represented at several hilltop sites elsewhere in the Teotihuacan Valley and the Basin of Mexico. West (196_) and Sanders, Parsons, and Santley (1979) ...  However, Bennyhoff (1967) is strongly of the opinion that it represents a distinct chronological period, between Cuanalan and Patlachique. If so, it implies that the TMP survey area was nearly unoccupied during an interval after occupation of the Cuanalan phase villages but before Patlachique phase reoccupation. The Tezoyuca phase will remain very poorly understood until more excavations are carried out in surviving sites of this phase in the Teotihuacan Valley and elsewhere.
