DF9Metadata_VarText: Patlachique phase. (Figure 3.x). The Patlachique phase (ca. 150 to 1 BC) is the first period for which large amounts of ceramics are found on the surfaces of many Teotihuacan sites – the period when Teotihuacan grew rapidly from almost nothing into a large city. Note that Figure 3.x does not include the sizable area of low-density Patlachique phase settlement northwest of the area covered by the intensive TMP survey, as discussed in Chapter One. Since neglect of this phase is so prevalent in the general Mesoamerican literature (for Pasztory [1997] it simply doesn’t exist), we emphasize that by the end of this phase Teotihuacan was already one of the largest settlements in Mesoamerica. DF9 records 27,524 sherds assigned to this phase. Cowgill's impression from having compared a large subset of the DF9 and Reanalysis tabulations – those for many of the cases where there was no doubt that the same collections were referred to – is that the total numbers of sherds assigned to the Patlachique-Tzacualli interval usually did not change greatly, but the proportion assigned to Patlachique changed considerably, and probably changed during the course of the reanalyses. At present he is not sure whether the reanalysis counts represent an improvement over those in DF9. The reanalysis total for Patlachique (data field 301[311]) is 42,331, an increase of about 61% over the DF9 count. Many sherds originally tabulated as Tzacualli were shifted to Patlachique during the ceramic reanalyses. Around 2000, Cowgill had the impression that there was a quite high level of concordance between what he and Zeferino Ortega identified as Patlachique. Nevertheless, it is clear that yet another analysis of Patlachique and Tzacualli ceramics in the TMP collections is badly needed in order to clarify key questions about the early growth of Teotihuacan, especially the rapidity of its growth and the spatial extent of substantial settlement during the Patlachique phase. (Look for Reans Data Sheets where the analysts filled in a matrix at the top of the form indicating for each phase how many sherds stayed in that phase & how many were shifted to each other phase.) Based on Cowgill's observations of the classification practices of Pedro Baños and Zeferino Ortega on ceramics from the Moon Pyramid and notes made by Mary Hopkins in February 1999 (personal communication), based on her observations of sherds in the Teotihuacan Archaeological Research Center type collections and on her interviews with Baños and Ortega, Cowgill suspects that the distinctions between Patlachique and Tzacualli in the DF9 tabulations are relatively accurate and based on criteria established by Bennyhoff, Millon, and Blucher; that at some time Rattray went off on a tangent and began classifying much that is really Tzacualli as Patlachique, thus skewing many of the reanalyses carried out by Andrea and Angela Ávila and perhaps some of those carried out by Baños and Ortega under Rattray's supervision. Possibly some of the later Baños and Ortega reanalyses reverted to the earlier (and in Cowgill's opinion, more accurate) criteria of Bennyhoff and Blucher. However, at present this is highly speculative and needs to be tested. [The "42% sample" in Chapter Two shows an increase of 165% of the Reans Patl total over the DF8 total, while the Reans Tzac total is only 49% of the DF8 total. The contour map published in Cowgill (1974:382) differs in details from the ca. 1981 map in ring binder, though the basic patterns are the same. The ring binder version shows a much more pronounced concentration (>200/ha) in N4W7. Both show somewhat localized >100/ha in N2W6 & a much broader concentration of >50/ha in N5W3, N5W2, N4W3, & N4W2, reaching >100/ha in parts of N5W2 & N4W2. Densities only 12-25/ha in vicinity of Moon, a localized peak of >50/ha at Sun, & a minor peak of ca. 6/ha in SE corner of the Ciudadela. The Ciudadela concentration is dubious in view of virtual absence of Patlachique in Feathered Serpent Pyramid ceramic analyses. The 1984 tabulation gives 528 in 8:N4W7, 454 in 11:N6W4, 310 in 3:N2W8, 384 in 18:N4W7, 257 in 7:N4W7, and 205 in 16:N4W7. All other DF9 cases have fewer than 200 Patlachique sherds. The basic point is really high densities on slopes of Cerro Colorado & Cerro Malinalco & extending beyond the mapped area, and another sizeable area of not quite such high densities in the "Inner Old City" – Plaza One is toward the northern edge of this district. The concentration in N6W4 is mainly due to 11:N6W4; next highest in this sector is L9:N6W4, with 80, then 4:N6W4 with 76, then 1A:N6W4 with 62.]. By any reckoning, it was during the Patlachique phase that, in one or two centuries, Teotihuacan grew from essentially nothing to a settlement occupied by some tens of thousands of people – already among the larger pre-Conquest settlements of Mesoamerica. In purely numerical terms, the resulting settlement might easily be considered "urban." The extent to which it was "urban" in terms of practices, institutions, and functions remains to be determined. Recent excavations at the Moon Pyramid (Cabrera and Sugiyama 1999) indicate that there was already a sizable platform or pyramid there in the Patlachique phase, measuring 23.5 by 23.5 m at the base. Its total height is unknown due to later disturbance. [Also Sugiyama & Cabrera 2006] It is unlikely that there was anything very large at the Sun Pyramid in this phase, and there certainly was not at the site of the later Ciudadela. No other interior of a Teotihuacan pyramid has been adequately explored, and we do not know the nature or extent of Patlachique phase civic-ceremonial structures.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Miccaotli phase. The DF9 total is 84,676 (Figure 3.x). It may seem disconcerting that this is a considerable decrease from the Tzacualli total. However, chronologies have tended to allocate a ca. 150-year time span to Tzacualli and ca. 200 years to the Tlamimilolpa phase, but only ca. 50 years to Miccaotli, that is, ca. AD 150 to 200. In terms of sherds per year, this implies a Miccaotli figure about 2.3 times that for Tzacualli, and 2.5 times that for Tlamimilolpa – in other words, a big Miccaotli spike in sherds per year. Such computations can never be taken as more than extremely rough guidelines for what is plausible about real-world phenomena, but they are among several reasons for thinking that Miccaotli ceramics were being produced for considerably more than a half century. Assigning something like a 120-year duration to the Miccaotli phase would bring it in line with Tzacualli and Tlamimilolpa sherds per year. These number games should not be carried far, however – they do not take the place of abundant high quality radiocarbon dates for inferring absolute chronologies. Nevertheless, Cowgill thinks it likely that the duration of the Miccaotli phase was more like a century than a half-century. For lack of anything better, he suggests adding a quarter-century at either end of earlier estimates and estimating the absolute date of the Miccaotli phase as ca. AD 125 to 225. Figure 3.x shows proportions of DF9 Miccaotli totals relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec sherds. Cowgill's preliminary investigations of ceramic reanalysis data indicate that there are some shifts between the DF9 Miccaotli identifications and those for Tzacualli, Tlamimilolpa, Xolalpan, and Metepec. Miccaotli shifts in identifications cover an unusually wide span of phases. Much of this may be due to Rattray's belief that hardly any Red or Red-on-natural ceramics date to the Miccaotli-Early Tlamimilolpa interval. Excavations such as those at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid cast doubt on this belief, since some Red-on-natural sherds were found there in contexts not later than Early Tlamimilolpa (Cowgill 1998; Cowgill and O. Cabrera 1991). (See what Rattray 2001 says about this.). Spatial patterns of Miccaotli sherd densities show a continuation of trends seen in the Tzacualli phase. Sherd densities are highest in the northwestern quadrant, especially in sectors N6W2 and eastern parts of N6W3 and N7W3, and in N4W2 and parts of N4W3 and N5W3. However, densities increase, relative to Tzacualli, in the southern and eastern quadrants of the city. The lobe of Patlachique and Tzacualli settlement northwest of the mapped area disappears.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Tlamimilolpa phase. DF9 shows 137,209 sherds for this phase (Figure 3.x). The phase as a whole perhaps lasted from about AD 225 to 350 (375?). A shortcoming of DF9 is that it does not distinguish Early Tlamimilolpa phase ceramics from those of the Late Tlamimilolpa phase. Contrary to what the names suggest, there is a much sharper break in styles and forms between the ceramics of Early Tlamimilolpa and Late Tlamimilolpa than between those of the Miccaotli and Early Tlamimilolpa phases. Most of the differences between Miccaotli and Early Tlamimilolpa ceramics are relatively subtle and not always easy to recognize with security. Indeed, Rattray (ref) has suggested, with good reason, that these three phases be renamed Early Miccaotli, Late Miccaotli, and Tlamimilolpa. For the present, however, we will stay with the old terminology. Use of molds for making figurines and composite censer ornaments begins or at least greatly increases. Earlier categories such as White-on-red decoration and vases with nubbin supports and outflaring rims disappear or become much scarcer. At the same time, forms such as ollas, cazuelas, flat-bottomed bowls with outcurving sides, and tapaplatos change more gradually and suggest considerable continuity in the local population. Thin Orange Ware and Granular Ware were imported both before and after the Early to Late Tlamimilolpa transition, although the volume of Thin Orange increases afterwards and the volume of Granular Ware may decrease. (Add some remarks about pastes, including from Hopkins?) The ceramic reanalyses also failed to distinguish between Early and Late Tlamimilolpa. At the time they were designed, Cowgill was not aware of how different these phases are. It is not clear why Rattray did not bring this to Cowgill's attention. Subsequently, Baños and Ortega have gone through the plastic bags of reanalyzed Tlamimilolpa sherds, tabulating the counts of Early and Late Tlamimilolpa sherds. (What is the status of creating an electronic file of these data & incorporating it w/ the Reans file?) Considering the Tlamimilolpa phase as a whole, the overall spatial distribution does not differ greatly from that for the Miccaotli phase. Figure 3.x shows proportions of DF9 Tlamimilolpa sherds relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec sherds. There is further infilling, especially toward the east, and higher densities in and near sectors N6W2 and N6W3.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Xolalpan phase. The DF9 total for this phase is 122,852 (Figure 3.x), somewhat less than the Tlamimilolpa phase total. The phase probably dates from around AD 350 [375?] to 550. Bennyhoff and Millon (n.d.) and Rattray (2001) recognize Early and Late subphases, but Cowgill has the impression that the differences are not great, and they are not distinguished in the tabulations of either DF9 or the reanalysis file. The decrease in sherd count relative to the Tlamimilolpa phase is too small to be taken seriously as an indication of population decline, but it certainly does not suggest any marked increase in population. Taking the different estimated durations of phases into account, sherd counts suggest a population plateau during the Miccaotli-Xolalpan interval – quite different from the Xolalpan peak postulated by Sanders et al. (1979) and others. The spatial pattern of Xolalpan phase sherd densities is, in general terms, similar to that for Tlamimilolpa. However, relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics, Xolalpan densities are notably high in the Tlajinga district (at least partly because of the high density of San Martín Orange Ware, which was manufactured in this district), somewhat high in the "Outer Old City" [rename?] (in and near N6W2 and N6W3), and in and near sectors N2W6, N2W1, N2E2, and N1W2. Xolalpan densities relative to total phased Miccaotli-Metepec tend to be low along the entire eastern margin of the city, along the Avenue of the Dead from the Moon Pyramid to somewhat south of the Sun Pyramid (where Miccaotli relative densities are above average), and in the Ciudadela (where Tlamimilolpa relative densities are above average) (Figure 3.x).

DF9Metadata_VarText: Metepec phase. The DF9 total is only 33,544 (Figure 3.x). Even taking into account estimates that this phase lasted only about a century (from ca. AD 550 to 650), this suggests a considerable population decline toward the end of Teotihuacan's existence. However, definitions of ceramic distinctions between Xolalpan and Metepec are still in flux, and it is possible that the population decline was less drastic than is suggested by the DF9 data. During the ceramic reanalyses there were appreciable switches between Metepec and Xolalpan and earlier phases, but the reanalysis tabulations for the Metepec phase should themselves be treated with considerable caution until more work on Metepec-phase materials has been carried out. Although ceramics identified as Metepec are never extremely abundant relative to those of other Miccaotli-Metepec phases, the highest relative proportions were identified in a small cluster of sites in the Metepec Hacienda district and, unexpectedly, in sector S2E1 (Figure 3.x). Proportions are also relatively high along the Avenue of the Dead from the Moon Pyramid to the Río San Juan, but not in the Ciudadela. Proportions are also rather high in and near N6E2, N4E2, N2W6 and N3W6, the Great Compound (N1W1), and a broad swath from there to the Tlajinga district. Low proportions are mostly near the city's margins, especially on the northwest. Most notably, this pattern does not suggest anything foreshadowing the partial abandonment of the core in later periods. Instead, it suggests greatest population decline around the margins and least decline in the central parts of the city.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Oxtoticpac phase. The DF9 total is 7,409 (Figure 3.x). Some workers, including Sanders (1986, 1989), who spells it Oxtotipac, following modern usage, regard this as a transitional phase between Metepec and Xometla. However, the Oxtoticpac phase is highly controversial and its very existence has been questioned by Rattray (1996, 2001?), who sees a marked discontinuity between Metepec and later ceramics at Teotihuacan. It is likely that ceramic analysts varied considerably in what, if anything, they recognized as belonging to this problematic phase. Many ceramic analysts may not have recognized an "Oxtoticpac" category at all, and put everything they recognized as Coyotlatelco-like into "Xometla." DF9 data field 214 is probably best combined with those for the Xometla phase (data field 215), and put into a generalized Coyotlatelco phase. This, indeed, is what was done in the ceramic reanalyses. It is likely that valid distinctions between Early and Late Coyotlatelco can eventually be made (Crider 2011), but both Cowgill and Rattray doubt whether these are captured by the DF9 tabulations.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Xometla phase. The DF9 total is 52,434 (Figure 3.x). As explained above, it would be best to group this data field with data field 214, leading to a Coyotlatelco total of 59,843 for DF9. Assuming (on the basis of quite limited evidence) that the Coyotlatelco phase lasted about two centuries, and that the Miccaotli-Metepec span perhaps lasted about 4.5 [4.75?] centuries (from ca. AD 150 [125?] to 600), this implies that the Coyotlatelco phase population may have been something like 3/10 the average Miccaotli-Metepec interval population [recompute] . This very rough estimate is not inconsistent with the total area of relatively dense to moderate Coyotlatelco sherd cover within the TMP survey area. Earlier population estimates by Sanders et al. (1979) and Diehl (1989) are based on far less evidence and/or poor understanding of the evidence and should be given little credence. (378,281/450=841 [excluding TO b/c it was collected more intensively]; 52,434/200=262; 262/841=0.31.) Neither DF9 nor the reanalysis file contain any information about Coyotlatelco ceramics other than the phase totals. Work by Destiny Crider (2002, 2011), based largely on TMP materials, greatly improves our understanding of the Coyotlatelco phase occupation in the TMP survey area. (Cite also various Rattray (esp. 1966 &1996) & other publications on Coyo & the Epiclassic.) Whether or not a transitional "Oxtoticpac" phase existed, the distribution pattern for Coyotlatelco ceramics as a whole differs very markedly from that of the Metepec phase. It is by far the most dramatic change in spatial pattern since the Patlachique phase, other than that due to the marked further spatial expansion in the Tzacualli phase. This great difference in the spatial pattern betokens, at least, a major social-political-religious reorganization. Some, including Rattray (1996) and Cowgill, believe that the stylistic discontinuities in ceramics are so great as to suggest a sizable in-migration, most likely from somewhere to the northwest. [Cite some refs.] The largest region of high Coyotlatelco sherd densities is in and for some distance around sectors N3W2, N4W2, and N4W3. Other concentrations are in northeastern S1W3; the Metepec Hacienda area in N1E7, where a Coyotlatelco obsidian workshop was excavated (Rattray 1983, 1987; Iceland need ref!1987c?), and in N3E3, where there is an even more pronounced concentration in the ensuing Mazapan phase. Coyotlatelco sherds are generally rather sparse near the Avenue of the Dead (especially at and near the Ciudadela), but this central area was not wholly unoccupied. There are, for example, some Coyotlatelco ceramics in the fill of 6C:N5W1, a structure immediately west of the Moon Pyramid [ref]. It is possible that a good deal of Coyotlatelco and later ceramics were summarily discarded during the 1962-64 INAH reconstruction of the façades of a number of structures along the Avenue of the Dead, but this cannot account for the scarcity of post-Teotihuacan Period ceramics on the unexcavated parts of these structures and on the surfaces of structures near the Avenue but not fronting on it.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Mazapan phase. The DF9 total is 41,732, not a great deal less than the Coyotlatelco total (Figure 3.x). Ceramics of this phase in the TMP collections have not yet received close study. The spatial pattern of densities shows some very general resemblances to that for the Coyotlatelco phase, but also marked differences. Notably, the concentration in N3E3 becomes more pronounced. This includes the site of Las Palmas, where George C. Vaillant dug in the early 1930s (his collections and records are at the American Museum of Natural History, still unpublished) and where Sigvald Linné (1934) worked more briefly. This district was probably the principal Mazapan phase settlement within the former urban zone of Teotihuacan. Weaker and more localized concentrations are in N5W3 and scattered elsewhere. Evidence of occupation in the area of the large Coyotlatelco phase concentration in and around N3W2 continues, but at greatly reduced density, and this was no longer a major focus of settlement. Mazapan sherd cover near the Avenue of the Dead is light. Cite relevant pubs, mention that McCullough (& Sanders, Nichols?) propose up to 5 phases between Metepec & Aztec.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Aztec phase. The DF9 total is 94,115 (Figure 3.x). A study of a sample of these materials by Christopher Garraty (1998, 2000) indicates that the vast majority are Late Aztec (Aztec III or IV, ca. 1350-1600) although some Early Aztec (Aztec II) occurs, notably in and around sector S3E6. Aztec I seems nearly or wholly absent [Get specifics from Chris]. There was a tendency for at least some field crews to under-collect Aztec feature sherds because of their great abundance. It may be that more Late Aztec sherds were generated per person per year than in earlier periods, and that Late Aztec materials are more visible on the surface. Even if so, these considerations do not seem to wholly account for the huge numbers of Late Aztec sherds observed or collected; comparable to the numbers for Teotihuacan Period phases of similar duration. Yet documents suggest that the local population on the eve of the Spanish Conquest was only about _____ to ______ [Look up figures, Sanders & Evans], far less than current estimates of the Teotihuacan Period population. This is one reason why Teotihuacan Period population estimates should be reconsidered. In spatial terms, Late Aztec sherd densities show continuation of broad Coyotlatelco and Mazapan phase trends. There is a broader area than before of extremely low sherd densities extending 500 to 1000 m on either side of the Avenue of the Dead, and at least some of the Aztec finds in this region suggest ritual activities rather than domestic activities (e.g., sherds in upper layers of the Plataforma Adosada observed by Cowgill in 1988, and an Aztec burial in the East Platform of the Ciudadela [ref]). Major Late Aztec sherd concentrations are more peripheral to the Teotihuacan Period urban zone than before, and occur in N6W3 and N7W3, N7W1 and N7E1 (all perhaps antecedents to present-day San Martín de las Pirámides); N1W6 (likely the main ancestor of the present town of San Juan Teotihuacán); S6W1 and S6E1; and S3E6. These last two are in sparsely settled farmlands today. Some of these peripheral concentrations extend at least somewhat beyond the mapped areas because they are outside the Teotihuacan urban zone, and funds for survey beyond this area were not available to the TMP, as explained in Chapter One. An analysis of selected TMP Aztec collections by Garraty (2000) offers a model of the Late Postclassic sociopolitical structure of Teotihuacan.
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Phased sherd totals. Troublesome problems for exact counts of certain specific categories generated by poorly documented removal of some "special" sherds from collections have little effect on phase totals, because the problematic sherds are such small proportions of phase totals. Both Bennyhoff and Rattray followed the practice, for most ceramic categories, of assigning sherds unequivocally to one phase or another, depending on the phase for which they seem most typical, and they trained other TMP ceramic analysts to do the same. Given that the TMP collections consist of feature sherds, this practice is less problematic than it would be if relatively featureless small body sherds were also included. Nevertheless, it results in some sherds being assigned to a phase on the basis of very strong evidence, while in other cases the phase assignment is a guess based on more ambiguous evidence. It also makes no allowance for the fact that a category highly typical of a specific phase may have begun to be produced in small amounts in the preceding phase and may have continued to be produced in small amounts in the following phase. These are far from fatal flaws, but they must be borne in mind in assessing chronological tabulations for specific sherd lots, from excavations as well as surface collections. The ceramic phase totals include all the specific phased categories listed in data fields following 217; that is to say, censers, San Martín Orange Ware, ollas, comales, nubbin supports, and Granular Ware, and also many phased sherds of categories not tabulated as such in DF9, including flat-bottomed outcurving bowls, vases, basins, cazuelas, floreros, and "Storm God" jars, among others. Many of these additional phased categories are tabulated in the reanalysis data file. The phased sherd totals do not include less well phased categories such as candeleros, burners, covers, Thin Orange, foreign wares other than Granular, and figurines. Corresponding phase totals for the ceramic reanalyses are given by data fields 300 to 309, in Chapter Four.

DF8Metadata_Text: Total censers, Patl-Met
DF9Metadata_VarText: Total Teotihuacan Period censers. DF9 records a total of 17,238 censer fragments (Figure 3.x). In addition at least some censer ornaments (adornos) are probably among the 1,143 objects tabulated under data field 274. Of the 17,238, 16,564 were assigned to a specific phase, and the remaining 674 were judged unphaseable by the analyst. Extremely few censer fragments were assigned to the Tzacualli or earlier phases. This may mean that censers (at least of Coarse Matte Ware) were very rare before Miccaotli, that a number of early censer fragments were incorrectly phased, and/or that some were of forms/wares not recognized as censers. (Esp puzzling is the scarcity of Tzac censers. Doesn't Rattray describe them as already in flanged-rim flowerpot tradition? Are there many Tzac censers in the Reans file?) The rim forms of Coarse Matte censer bowls have proven highly sensitive and excellent time markers. They all have flanges or bolsters, but the cross-sections, degrees of overhang, and widths of flanges vary over time. In earlier phases, many of the flanges have circular or semi-circular impressions in the wet clay, and the forms and spacing of these impressions vary over time. In later phases the flanges are generally smoothed and plain, although in a few cases modeled clay elements are attached. Very rarely, these show motifs derived from the Maya area (Taube 2000:____). Figures 3.x to 3.x show censer bowl flanges typical of each phase. These flowerpot-like censer bowls often had pedestal supports and always had lids. In earlier phases the lids seem generally to be rather simple, but by the (Early Tla???) phase they often consist of a tall cylindrical chimney and a rather elaborate clay armature to which a profusion of molded clay ornaments (adornos) were attached. These are the "composite" or "theatre" censers for which Teotihuacan is famed. In earlier phases the adornos are hand-modeled, but by the (Late Tlamimilolpa?) phase they are typically mold-made. Specific adorno motifs and stylistic variants may prove to be good time markers. Censer bowl body sherds are usually unphaseable and, indeed, indistinguishable from three-prong burner bodies (data field 201). This is not a major problem for the TMP surface collections because featureless body sherds were rarely collected, but it leads to many Coarse Matte body sherds from excavations being put into an ambiguous and largely unphaseable "burner/censer" category. For more on Teotihuacan censers in general, see Rattray (2001). Langley (1986, 1991, 1992, 1993) has studied censer adorno motifs extensively. Múnera (1985) and Sugiyama and Múnera (in press) discuss and catalog a large collection of censer adornos and adorno molds excavated by the Proyecto Arqueológico Teotihuacan 80-82 in site 2:N1E1, within a large walled enclosure attached to the north side of the Ciudadela. Teotihuacan-derived composite censers, all or nearly all of local manufacture, are rather abundant in highland and coastal Guatemala and have been discussed especially by Berlo (1984, 1989), Bove (1986), Bove and Medrano (2003), and Hellmuth (1975). Teotihuacan-like composite censers seem curiously uncommon elsewhere, even in sites where other evidences of Teotihuacan connections are clear.

DF8Metadata_Text: Mic censers
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Miccaotli through Metepec phase censers.  The DF9 totals are, respectively, 3,900, 6,374, 5,244, and 964. For Miccaotli through Xolalpan, these counts are steadily 4-5% of total phased sherds, but for Metepec censers they are a little less than 3% of the total. This might suggest a slight decline in use of composite censers (together with increasing use of tapaplatos?), but it may simply reflect problems in criteria for the Metepec phase. In terms of spatial distribution, there is a very marked concentration in the "Outer Old City" district (Figures 3.x to 3.x). Even taking into account the high absolute densities of Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics in this district, the relative proportion of censers is exceptionally high. It is above 6% of total Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics in a large area that includes N7W3, N7W2, N6W4, N6W3, N6W2, and N5W3 (Figure 3.x). This same pattern appears when Tlamimilolpa phase censers are considered relative to total Tlamimilolpa ceramics (Figure 3.x), and when Xolalpan phase censers relative to total Xolalpan ceramics are mapped (Figure 3.x). It is, thus, a stable pattern over time. These unusually high proportions suggest the possibility that censers were manufactured in this district, but so far the only place where censer manufacture has been confirmed is in site 2:N1E1, just north of the Ciudadela, as discussed above. Elsewhere there are only a few spots where relative proportions exceed 6%, including just south of the Hacienda Metepec area in sector N1E7.  In much of the city, relative proportions are only in the 2-3% range, which shows how the overall average of 4-5% masks considerable spatial variation. Relative proportions are below 1.4% in a number of districts, many near the city margins but including some areas on and near the Avenue of the Dead. The spatial distribution of composite censers does not suggest that they were especially important in activities associated with major civic-ceremonial structures. It is more likely that they were used in rituals involving occupants of individual apartment compounds, perhaps especially for commemoration of and communion with dead ancestors.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Regular Thin Orange Ware. The DF9 total is 88,305 (Figure 3.x). This is what is usually simply called Thin Orange Ware, but we add the term "Regular" to distinguish it from a much less abundant "Coarse" variant. Note that the total is roughly 18% of the Miccaotli through Metepec sherd total in DF9, but this is very misleading because, as explained in Chapter Two, even plain body sherds of Thin Orange Ware were collected. A more realistic estimate of the proportion of Regular Thin Orange sherds to all Miccaotli-Metepec sherds would be about __ percent, based on the intensive collections from a few sites described in Chapter Two. Rattray (1981) illustrates many Thin Orange forms and makes estimates of changing proportions of Thin Orange Ware over time, based on excavations. [I believe that Millon is very critical of Kolb's (1973, 1984, & 1986) publications on TO, but they ought to be checked and mentioned] DF9 gives no information on shapes (these are provided in the reanalysis file, data fields 310-319), but the vast majority are rather standardized hemispherical bowls with ring bases (Figure 3.x), often plain, but sometimes with incised or incised and punctate decorations. These bowls begin to appear at Teotihuacan at least by the Late Tzacualli phase, and become more abundant later. Regular Thin Orange disappears at or near the end of Metepec, although small amounts of variants may persist a little later (reference if possible). So far it has not been possible to identify phase variants among the bowls. They differ strikingly in shape and decorative motifs from Teotihuacan forms (until some apparent imitations in Burnished Ware bowls were made in the Metepec phase), as well as in paste and temper. Perhaps the next most common forms are bowls with outcurving rims (Figure 3.x), also atypical of locally-made Teotihuacan forms. Other forms are less common and some, such as direct-rim cylinder tripod vases, do resemble local Teotihuacan forms. One highly unusual form (Figure 3.x) was found at Tlachinolpan (off the TMP map, in sector N7W8) and apparently dates to the Patlachique phase (Blucher 1971). It was long suspected that Regular Thin Orange Ware was made somewhere in southern Puebla, and Rattray (1990) confirmed this with excavations at a site near Tepexi del Río, some __ km from Teotihuacan. In spite of its distant source, it is so abundant and widespread all over Teotihuacan that it is clear that the hemispherical bowls, at least, were used by a very broad segment of the population. Relative to total Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics, the highest proportions occur, unexpectedly, near the western margins of the city (Figure 3.x). Reexamination of some of these collections by Cowgill shows that many Regular Thin Orange sherds in this district, as well as elsewhere in the city, show use-wear, so these high proportions in a marginal part of the city cannot be due to Thin Orange having been merely warehoused there. There is also an east-west band of somewhat high relative proportions running from the vicinity of the Moon Pyramid in N5W1 for about 1.5 km, into N4E2. Proportions are only average elsewhere in central parts of the city. Cowgill would have expected this imported ware, although obviously shared by households spanning a wide range of socioeconomic statuses, to have formed a somewhat higher proportion of the inventories of higher status households. Work by Robertson (2001, 2005, and in press) suggests that higher status residences are more prevalent near the center of the city. The failure of the spatial distribution pattern of Regular Thin Orange to conform to Cowgill's expectation is perplexing (Cowgill 1987). Perhaps Thin Orange hemispherical bowls were not very costly, as suggested by the huge volume in which they were imported. Thin Orange hemispherical bowls were probably used a good deal as serving vessels, but many show abrasion on the interior bottom, strongly suggesting that one of their uses was as molcajetes in preparation of food (and possibly other materials) by grinding. This is made more likely by the fact that ceramic molcajetes with incisions on the bottom are not part of the Teotihuacan Period ceramic repertoire. Similar abrasion is rarely if ever seen on the interior bases of Teotihuacan Burnished ware vessels. This evidence of a utilitarian function for Thin Orange hemispherical bowls is another suggestion that they were not terribly costly. Perhaps something about the fabric of Regular Thin Orange ware made it seem preferable to the Teotihuacanos for grinding activities. This might be explored by experimentation. Rattray (ref) has suggested that these hemispherical bowls may have been used as supports for spindles used in spinning, but this seems unlikely because of the scarcity of evidence for spinning at Teotihuacan (O. Cabrera 1999 [2001?] ) and because, at least in Cowgill's opinion, the abrasion patterns do not look like they had been made by rotating spindles. Some Regular Thin Orange Ware is quite thin, especially in small vessels, but the majority of cases are only somewhat thinner than locally-made Teotihuacan wares; about 5-6 mm. (check). Indeed, some Thin Orange vessels were enormous, including great cauldrons over a meter in diameter, with walls over a centimeter thick, which must have been a challenge to transport from southern Puebla. These are a variant called, logically enough, Thick Thin Orange. Thick Thin Orange was not tabulated separately from Regular Thin Orange in DF9, but it was tabulated separately in the ceramic reanalyses (data field 312), although, due to a design error in the tabulation form, it is sometimes hard to tell whether the analyst meant "Thick" Thin Orange or "Coarse" Thin Orange. Outside Teotihuacan, Regular Thin Orange has often been taken as a sign of a Teotihuacan connection. This may be so, for Teotihuacan may have controlled manufacture and distribution of the ware. But it also seems quite possible that the producers of Regular Thin Orange, although they supplied a very large demand from Teotihuacan, may have acted independently in supplying the ware to other customers, and these other customers may or may not have especially valued the ware because of its associations with Teotihuacan. These are issues that need further exploration. (Add more, including studies by Sotomayor & Kolb, INAA (including Cowgill & Neff 2001), composition & geology. Charlton on apparent trade routes, Drennan et al., Stark et al.)

DF8Metadata_Text: Coarse Thin Orange
DF9Metadata_VarText: Coarse Thin Orange Ware. The DF9 total is 8,372 (Figure 3.x). The fabric is similar to Regular Thin Orange (any compositional studies to refer to? Any reason to think any of it made at Teo? Or not made at same place as RTO?) but the temper is much coarser and the surface finish much rougher. Many Coarse Thin Orange vessels were amphoras, and Rattray (2001:__) believes the ware is restricted to the Metepec phase. However, excavations at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid in 1988-89 (refs) revealed a few sherds of Coarse Thin Orange Ware not later than the Early Tlamimilolpa phase, although they were too small to tell whether they came from amphoras or other forms. Spatially, highest proportions of Coarse Thin Orange relative to total phased Xolalpan-Metepec ceramics occur in a large zone from N1E6 to N1E9 (Figure 3.x). The proportion relative to total Thin Orange Ware is also notably high in this district (Figure 3.x). Data field 313 gives reanalysis counts of Coarse Thin Orange.

DF8Metadata_Text: Total San Martin Orange (SMO) Ware. It is unlikely that any SMO is really Tla, and probably quite a bit of what is coded Xol here is really Met. Pending results from the reanalyses, it is best to use only var.233 for SMO.
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: San Martín Orange Ware. A total of 54,550 sherds of San Martín Orange Ware are recorded in DF9 (Figure 3.x). This is a locally made utility ware. DF9Metadata_VarText: Teotihuacan Period ollas.  These are in what Rattray (2001) calls Burnished Ware. They come in a variety of sizes and shapes, used for transport, storage, and cooking (Figure 3.x). They all have rounded neck-body junctions and rounded bases. A variety of lip and neck forms have considerable chronological significance, although changes are gradual, suggesting strong cultural continuity but also making judgments between two consecutive subphases difficult. A total of 74,875 Teotihuacan period olla fragments are recorded in DF9 (Figure 3.x?). Several times as many were recorded in the ceramic reanalyses (data fields 320-329). The reason why far fewer were recorded in the earlier analyses is not entirely clear, but it is likely that the earlier analyses (represented by DF9) counted only the larger olla rims, while the reanalyses also count rims of smaller vessels – what some might call "jars." However, in describing Teotihuacan ceramic forms, it is better to reserve the term "jar" for a quite different form, often of "Polished" Ware, unlikely to have been used for transport, storage, or cooking, and more likely used as serving vessels and perhaps for some rituals, with tall, outcurving necks, sharp neck-body junctions, flat bottoms, and often with solid nubbin supports [Figure 3.x]. These polished jars are among the many forms that are included in DF9 phase totals but not tabulated separately. For more information about jars, see reanalysis data fields 331-334, 366-369, 389-392, and 479. Burnished ollas were perhaps made by unspecialized potters in a number of spatially scattered household workshops. However, this is yet another hypothesis about ceramic manufacture at Teotihuacan that remains to be tested. No definite Teotihuacan olla manufacturing site has yet been identified. Burnished ollas must have served for many of the same uses as San Martín Orange Ware and may have been cheaper and used in higher proportions by poorer households. Robertson (2001) shows that sites with highest proportions of Miccaotli and Tlamimilolpa ollas are more prevalent in the outer parts of the city, and these are districts with other ceramic indicators of relatively low socioeconomic status. This very likely is the case also in later phases. It will be extremely interesting to apply Robertson's methods to the Xolalpan and Metepec phases, when both burnished ollas and San Martín Orange vessels were used in quantity. [Also I should try principal components analysis and/or correspondence analysis.] One would think that if whole Teotihuacan families moved abroad in any numbers they would recreate Teotihuacan-style ollas using local clays. Teotihuacan style ollas outside the immediate Teotihuacan core area have not been reported, but perhaps it is because Teotihuacan olla forms were not widely known before Rattray's (2001) publication. On the other hand, if the only Teotihuacano categories of people who moved abroad were those not likely to have known how to make pottery, such as soldiers, male merchants, and elites, it is likely that they would have been most concerned about the local production of close replicas of Teotihuacan-style ceremonial and elite objects and they may have left production of utilitarian ceramics to local potters using local forms and styles.

DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Comales. DF9 records a total of 7,925. All the sherds in this category are rims of very flat plates, but it is not certain that all were used as comales, i.e., griddles. Only six objects were catalogued as Tzacualli comales (data field 246), and none as Patlachique (data field 245). Quite possibly comales did not exist in these phases. Counts for later phases are Miccaotli, 1,463 (Figure 3.x); Tlamimilolpa, 2,274 (Figure 3.x); Xolalpan, 3,433 (Figure 3.x), Metepec, 630 (Figure 3.x); Oxtoticpac, 11; and post-Oxtoticpac, none. These last two counts should be ignored, the Oxtoticpac count because of the problems about this putative phase discussed above, and the later phases because in fact numerous post-Teotihuacan comales occur in the TMP collections, especially Aztec comales, but, like all other specific categories for the Coyotlatelco, Mazapan, and Aztec periods, were hardly ever recorded in DF9. There are enough comal fragments dated to the Miccaotli-Metepec interval to make it likely that tortillas were already a significant item of diet by the Miccaotli phase, although probably considerably less so than in the sixteenth century. There is some uncertainty about comal phasing within the Miccaotli-Metepec interval. (Discuss separate investigations of their phasing by Cowgill (DF8) and Robertson (Reans?). This should also be discussed for several other phased categories.).

DF8Metadata_Text: Total nubbins
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Nubbin vessel supports. The DF9 total is 10,430. These are small solid conical or button-like supports that occur on flat-bottomed outcurving bowls and vases (nearly always with outflaring lips – Figure 109 of Berrin and Pasztory [1993:236-37] is an exception).  Polished jars also often have nubbin supports, but polished jars themselves are rather rare. Exceedingly few nubbin supports occur on any other Teotihuacan forms. Shouldered hollow supports with circular sections and pointed bottoms occur in the Cuanalan phase (Figure 3.x) and probably continue in small proportions in the Patlachique phase, but these are not nubbins and they would not have been tabulated in DF9, if any at all were found by the TMP survey. The 27 "Patlachique" nubbins (data field 254) may be correct or may be in error. Vessel supports of any kind seem to have been absent in the Tzacualli phase, and data field 255 should be ignored. Nubbin supports are quite common on vases and outcurving bowls in the Miccaotli and Early Tlamimilolpa phases, while other kinds of supports in those phases are uncommon. Nubbin supports thereafter become scarcer and increasingly vestigial. At one time it was thought that nubbin supports set slightly inward from base-side junctions (data field 256, 4,151 cases, Figure 3.x) were markers of the Miccaotli phase and nubbins set flush with the junctions (with burnishing streaks often continuing from the vessel side onto the nubbin) (data field 257, 5,736 cases, Figure 3.x) were diagnostic of the Early Tlamimilolpa phase. This is now considered questionable, but the distinction may yet prove to have some chronological significance. Any consideration of "inset" versus "flush" should, however, consider bowls, vases, and jars separately. Data field 258 ("Atoyac" nubbins) should not be used. The very low counts of data field 259, Xolalpan nubbins (45), and data field 260, Metepec nubbins (155), may reflect a tendency of ceramic analysts to assign nubbins to earlier phases unless there was strong evidence otherwise. However, there is no doubt that flat-bottomed outcurving bowls much more often lacked supports of any kind in these later phases. Surprisingly, the coding forms that became the basis for DF9 were not set up so as to record any other kinds of vessel supports, including the rounded and slab supports so common on Teotihuacan direct-rim cylinder vases. This was one of the many omissions in the early ceramic analyses that the reanalyses were designed to correct.

Shouldered hollow supports with circular sections and pointed bottoms occur in the Cuanalan phase (Figure 3.x) and probably continue in small proportions in the Patlachique phase, but these are not nubbins and they would not have been tabulated in DF9, if any at all were found by the TMP survey. The 27 "Patlachique" nubbins (data field 254) may be correct or may be in error. Vessel supports of any kind seem to have been absent in the Tzacualli phase, and data field 255 should be ignored. Nubbin supports are quite common on vases and outcurving bowls in the Miccaotli and Early Tlamimilolpa phases, while other kinds of supports in those phases are uncommon. Nubbin supports thereafter become scarcer and increasingly vestigial. At one time it was thought that nubbin supports set slightly inward from base-side junctions (data field 256, 4,151 cases, Figure 3.x) were markers of the Miccaotli phase and nubbins set flush with the junctions (with burnishing streaks often continuing from the vessel side onto the nubbin) (data field 257, 5,736 cases, Figure 3.x) were diagnostic of the Early Tlamimilolpa phase. This is now considered questionable, but the distinction may yet prove to have some chronological significance. Any consideration of "inset" versus "flush" should, however, consider bowls, vases, and jars separately. Data field 258 ("Atoyac" nubbins) should not be used. The very low counts of data field 259, Xolalpan nubbins (45), and data field 260, Metepec nubbins (155), may reflect a tendency of ceramic analysts to assign nubbins to earlier phases unless there was strong evidence otherwise. However, there is no doubt that flat-bottomed outcurving bowls much more often lacked supports of any kind in these later phases. Surprisingly, the coding forms that became the basis for DF9 were not set up so as to record any other kinds of vessel supports, including the rounded and slab supports so common on Teotihuacan direct-rim cylinder vases. This was one of the many omissions in the early ceramic analyses that the reanalyses were designed to correct.

DF9Metadata_VarText: Stuccoed sherds. 121 (Figure 3.x). Stuccoed sherds are from vessels with polychrome decoration applied on a post-firing fine calcareous layer. Conides (2001) is a particularly important study of relatively complete examples of this kind of decoration [On cylinder tripod vases only? Check.] They are among the finest and presumably most costly Teotihuacan-Period vessels and presumably most abundant in the refuse from high status households. They are probably considerably under-represented in the TMP surface collections because the stucco is quite fragile and easily lost during post-deposition vicissitudes. The small number found in surface survey makes them of limited value for interpreting specific sites, because many sites where none were collected would probably reveal examples if they were extensively excavated. However, the DF9 data are useful for identifying general districts where they were found in above average proportions.

DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Foreign sherds.  Excluding Thin Orange Ware and Granular Ware (foreign categories that were abundant, readily recognizable, and tabulated separately), 2,171 sherds were identified as foreign in DF9. Of these, 1,521 were merely identified as probably foreign, with no attempt to guess a place of origin. When such guesses were made, it is not clear how well-informed they were. In any case, Rattray (personal communication) reports that she has identified about five to ten times as many foreign sherds in the TMP collections as are tabulated in DF9, but she has not yet made her tabulations available to us, and this means that data fields 265-273 are of very limited value. It is clear, however, that ceramics from west Mexico, Oaxaca, the Gulf lowlands, and the Lowland Maya area were reaching Teotihuacan, in addition to Thin Orange Ware from southern Puebla and Granular Ware, perhaps from Guerrero. Other sources may well be represented also. Rattray (1987a) shows hard-to-read maps of distribution of some foreign sherd categories, and Rattray (1979a) is an unpublished manuscript with extensive discussions of foreign sherd categories believed to come from various parts of the Gulf Lowlands, based in part on an unpublished report of neutron activation analyses by Sayre and Harbottle (1979). Clayton (2003) reports on results of INAA analyses of 121 Maya sherds in the TMP collections carried out by Ron Bishop at the Smithsonian Institution. These include some from TMP excavations in the Merchants' Enclave. Other publications on foreign ceramics at Teotihuacan include Rattray (1978, 1979b, 1990, 1993) and Cowgill and Neff (2001).

DF8Metadata_Text: Total Granular Ware. Var.278 is good. The phasing for granular ware is now considered uncertain, so vars.279-283 should be used with great caution, if at all. Note that granular ware almenas are recorded separately, as var.28.
DF9Metadata_VarGroupText: Granular Ware. This is a very distinctive foreign ware, easily recognized by appearance and feel. DF9 data field 278 records a total of 12,592 (Figure 3.x). Next to Thin Orange Ware, it is the second most abundant foreign ceramic at Teotihuacan, and far more abundant than ceramics from any other non-local source. Nearly all examples are in the form of sizable amphoras, often with three loop handles (Figure 3.x). Surfaces are matte, and there is often rather bold, sloppy decoration in reddish, pinkish, or black paint that is dull rather than lustrous, with styles and motifs untypical of locally made wares. They have the look of quite utilitarian vessels for transporting or storing liquids. It has been suggested that they were a preferred kind of vessel for storing drinking water because the fabric may be porous enough to allow some water to seep through, evaporate from the exterior, and hence cool the contents (since considerable heat energy is absorbed by the evaporation of water). This suggestion is plausible enough, especially since slightly porous vessels are used in this way today in Mexico and in many other parts of the world, but, so far as I know, it has not been tested experimentally. If it is confirmed that the fabric works better for this purpose than do fabrics of vessels made from Teotihuacan Valley clays, it would explain why this utilitarian form was imported in such quantities. Neutron activation analysis (e.g., Cowgill and Neff 2001) and other studies confirm unequivocally that Granular Ware is of foreign origin. The exact source has not been identified, but similar wares (not necessarily in the same shapes) are reported elsewhere, and it is likely that the source is somewhere in western Morelos or eastern Guerrero. [Cite recent tesis by student of Paul Schmidt] Data fields 279-283 purport to record phase totals (501 pre-Miccaotli, 5,155 Miccaotli, 5,600 Tlamimilolpa, 1,183 Xolalpan, and 9 Metepec). However, the phasing of Granular Ware is highly uncertain, and these numbers should be treated with great caution. Nevertheless, stratigraphic evidence at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid shows that Granular Ware was already being imported at least as early as Early Tlamimilolpa (Cowgill 1998), and various statistical studies suggest that its import began by Tzacualli times and very likely declined in volume by the Xolalpan phase or even earlier. The spatial distribution of highest proportions relative to total Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics is rather unusual – it is above 3.5% in a broad zone in the northwest running from N6W3 to N6W1 and south to N3W3, in the far south from S4E1 to S7E1, and in a few other places; and above 7% in a strip running northeast from N5W3 to N6W1 (Figure 3.x). Proportions are only average (1-3%) in most of the central part of the city and below 1% in collections from the Ciudadela, the Great Compound, and much of the easternmost parts of the city. These spatial variations in proportions of Granular Ware relative to total Miccaotli-Metepec ceramics make some sense if we assume that much of the Granular Ware total was imported in Tzacualli and Miccaotli times. Ceramic roof ornaments (almenas), data field 28, appear visually to have also been made of Granular Ware, although some almenas are made of stone (probably counted under data field 135 or 146). [Granular Ware doesn't appear in the reanalysis file. It surely must be on the reanalysis data sheets, but probably wasn't phased, and Cowgill probably felt there was no strong need to check the Granular totals in the original analyses.]

DF8Metadata_Text: Structure area. Coded "-1" or "0" if no structure is shown on the red "Interpretations" sheet in Millon et al. (1973) or if there are only conventionalized symbols for insubstantial structures. Otherwise, it is a 4-digit variable recording approximately the area (in square meters) of apartment compounds, temples, platforms, and other substantial structures. However, 14 sites are coded "9999," indicating that the actual area was 10,000 square meters or more. The cumulative total is 5,527,199 square meters, or 552.72 hectares, or 5.527 square kilometers, but this does not represent the full area of the 14 largest structures, including the Sun Pyramid, which is far more than 10,000 square meters.
DF9Metadata_VarText: Structure area. This is based on the structures shown in red in the transparent "interpretations" overlay sheets in Millon et al. (1973) and is a more meaningful estimate of ancient structure size than is the collection tract area (data field 203). It records the area, in square meters, of substantial structures believed to have been occupied during the Xolalpan phase. it includes civic-ceremonial and other structures as well as substantial residential structures. Insubstantial structure areas are shown as "missing data" because the red rectangles for these on the "interpretations" sheets are merely conventional symbols. Because of the fixed-field format of early predecessors of DF8, areas only up to 9,999 m2 could be recorded accurately. In DF9, 14 cases are coded "9999," which means that the structure area is some unknown amount greater than 9,999 m2. These include the Sun Pyramid (about 48,870 m2) and the Moon Pyramid (about 21,420 m2), among others. Data field 289 sums to 5,527,199 m2, or 552.72 ha, or 5.527 km2. Including the fractions of the areas of the Sun and Moon in excess of 9,999 m2 brings the total to over 5.577 km2, still a slightly conservative estimate since it does not include the excess over 9,999 m2 of the other 12 cases. This total is considerably less than the meaningful area of the city because it does not include streets and avenues, insubstantial structures, plazas, and other open spaces between structures. Summing the total area of residential structures could be relevant for estimating the city's population, but cannot substitute for more careful consideration of structure layouts in making population estimates.
